items.title: DF oo ballan-qaad u sameysay ardaydii kaalmaha hore ka galay tartankii Qatar
items.description: Muqdisho (Caasimada Online) – Ra’iisul Wasaaraha Soomaaliya Mudane Xamza Cabdi Barre oo Tallaabadii xafiiskiisa ku qaabilay saddexda ardey ee kaalmaha hore ka galay Tartanka Qur’aanka Kariimka, oo dhawaan lagu qabtay Dalka Qatar ayaa u sameeyay ballan-qaad culus. Tartankan oo ay ka qeyb galeen 398 arday oo ka kala yimid 20 Dal ayaa waxaa kaalinta 1aad ka galay Qaari Cabdiqani Cabdulqaadir Sheekh Xuseen, Qaari Cabdiraxmaan Qaasim Maxamed ayaa isna galay kaalinta 2aad halka Qaari Cabdiraxmaan Axmed Maxamuud uu galay kaalinta 3aad, waxaana ka qeybgalkooda fududeysay Hay’adda Qatar Charity. Ra’iisul Wasaare Xamza ayaa ku bogaadiyey dhallinyaradan dadaalkooda iyo sida ay Qur’aanka u xafideen, isagoo kula dardaarmay in dadka ay baraan Qur’aanka Kariimka. Sidoo kale, Ra’iisul Wasaaraha ayaa sheegay in Dowladdu dhiirri galineyso barashada Qur’aanka Kariimka waxaana uu u ballan-qaaday ardeyda in dowladdu siineyso waxbarasho lacag la’aan ah sidii ay u siisay ardeydii kaalimaha hore ka gashay Imtixaankii Shahaadiga ah. “Waan idinku faaneynaa haddii aan nahay Madaxda Dowladda, in Tartan dowli ah aad ka gasheen kaalimaha 1aad, 2aad iyo 3aad waa arrin wanaagsan oo sharaf iyo Karaamo u ah Bulshada Soomaaliyeed, Wasaaradda Waxbarashada waxaan fari doonaa in Waxbarasho bilaash ah ay idin siiso,” ayuu yiri Ra’iisul wasaare Xamza. Si kastaba ha’ahaatee, Ballan-qaadkan ayaa ah mid lagu dhiirrigelinayo ardayda Soomaaliyeed ee dadaalka geliya barashada iyo xifdinta Qur’aanka Kariimka, gaar ahaan kuwa dalka ku metela tartamada caalamiga ah. Saddexda arday ayaa guushan ku soo kordhiyay sumcad iyo sharaf ay ku faani karaan bulshada Soomaaliyeed, kaddib markii ay kaalimaha hore ka galeen tartan ay ka qeybgaleen arday badan oo ka kala socday dalal kala duwan. Dowladda Federaalka Soomaaliya ayaa dhankeeda sidoo kale sheegtay inay sii wadi doonto dhiirrigelinta ardayda Soomaaliyeed ee guulaha ka gaara tartamada iyo imtixaannada heer qaran iyo heer caalami. The post DF oo ballan-qaad u sameysay ardaydii kaalmaha hore ka galay tartankii Qatar appeared first on Caasimada Online .

items.title: Soomaaliya iyo Midowga Afrika oo xoojinaya iskaashiga amniga + Sawirro
items.description: Muqdisho (Caasimada Online) – La-taliyaha Amniga Qaranka ayaa maanta magaalada Muqdisho kusoo gaba-gabeeyay kulamo u dhexeeyay hay’adaha Dowladda Federaalka Soomaaliya iyo xarunta la-dagaallanka argagixisada ee Midowga Afrika. Kulanka maanta ayaa lagu soo koobay wada-tashiyadii iyo kulamadii labada maalmood ee lasoo dhaafay, iyadoo dhinacyadu ay dib u eegis ku sameeyeen arrimihii lagu falanqeeyay kulamadaas. Xarunta la-dagaallanka argagixisada ee Midowga Afrika ayaa Dowladda Federaalka Soomaaliya, gaar ahaan Xafiiska Amniga Qaranka uga mahadcelisay soo dhaweynta iyo fududeynta kulamadii ay la yeelatay hay’adaha kala duwan ee dowladda. Wafdiga Xarunta ayaa sidoo kale bogaadiyay horumarka ay Dowladda Federaalka Soomaaliya ka sameysay dhinaca la-dagaallanka argagixisada. Kulamada ayaa diiradda lagu saaray xoojinta wada-shaqeynta dhinacyada amniga iyo la-dagaallanka argagixisada, iyadoo la is dhaafsaday aragtiyo iyo khibrado la xiriira wax-ka-qabashada khataraha amni ee ka jira gobolka. Dhinaca Midowga Afrika ayaa carrabka ku adkeeyay muhiimadda ay leedahay in la sii xoojiyo iskaashiga kala dhexeeya Soomaaliya, gaar ahaan dhinacyada la xiriira ka-hortagga iyo la-dagaallanka argagixisada. Xafiiska Amniga Qaranka ayaa kulamada la yeeshay hay’adaha kala duwan ee dowladda, iyadoo ujeeddadu ahayd in la xoojiyo isku-duwidda dadaallada Soomaaliya iyo kuwa Midowga Afrika ee la xiriira amniga. Wafdiga xarunta la-dagaallanka argagixisada ee Midowga Afrika ayaa ugu dambeyn sheegay in sii wadista wada-shaqeynta iyo iskaashiga ay muhiim u yihiin horumarinta dadaallada looga hortagayo argagixisada iyo khataraha amni ee gobolka. The post Soomaaliya iyo Midowga Afrika oo xoojinaya iskaashiga amniga + Sawirro appeared first on Caasimada Online .

items.title: Wararkii ugu dambeeyay dibad-baxyo ka dhacay Koonfur Galbeed oo Turkiga…
items.description: Baydhaba (Caasimada Online) – Dowlad-goboleedka Koonfur Galbeed Soomaaliya ayaa taageero xoogan u muujisay Turkiga, kadib markii deegaanno ka tirsan maamulkaas iyo qaybo kamid ah Jubbaland lagu gubay calanka Turkiga. Dibad-baxyo balaaran oo saacadihii lasoo dhaafay ka dhacay inta badan degmooyinka Koonfur Galbeed ayaa garab istaagga buuxa loogu muujiyay dowladda Turkiga oo ah saaxibka koowaad ee Soomaaliya. Dadka ka qayb-galay dibadbaxa ayaa soo qaatay calanka Turkiga iyo boorar ay ku xardhan yihiin erayo ay ku taageerayaan garab istaagga Turkiga. Qaar kamid ah dibadb-baxayaasha oo la hadlay warbaahinta ayaa dareenkooda cabiray, iyaga oo sheegay inay abaal u ahayaan madaxweyne Erdogan iyo dowladdiisa oo xilli adag usoo gurmaday Soomaaliya. “Banaanbaxaynu cambaareyn ma’aha tageero waayay Turkiga abaal wayn ayuu nagu leeyahay xilligii aan u baahnayn ayuuna garab istaag noo muujiyay,” ayay tiri hooyo kamid ah ururka haweenka ee Baydhaba. Sidoo kale, waxaa dibadbaxa ka qayb-galay guddoomiyeyaasha gobollada iyo kuwa degmooyinka oo fagaare kula hadlay shacabka isku soo baxay, waxayna sidoo kale ka hadleen falkii lagu gubay calanka Turkiga oo ay cambaareeyeen. “Falalka ay geysteen dad aan garanayn qiimaha xiriirka labada dal ma wiiqi karaan saaxiibtinimada iyo xiriirka qotada dheer ee ka dhexeeya Soomaaliya iyo Turkiga,” ayuu yiri Guddoomiyaha Gobolka Bakool, Maxamed Axmed. Koonfur Galbeed ayaa hadda wajaheyso xaalad adag, waxayna dagaal kula jirtaa ciidamada taabacsan Cabdicasiis Lafta-gareen oo ku sugan bannaanka magaalada Baydhaba, halkaas oo kasoo abaabulaan weerarro qorsheysan. The post Wararkii ugu dambeeyay dibad-baxyo ka dhacay Koonfur Galbeed oo Turkiga… appeared first on Caasimada Online .

items.title: Ururka Iskaashiga Islaamka oo cambaareeyay weerarrada Xuutiyiinta ee Maka iyo Madiina
items.description: Xoghaynta Guud ee Ururka Iskaashiga Islaamka (OIC) ayaa si adag u cambaareysay weerarro ay sheegtay in kooxda Xuutiyiinta ay ku qaaday magaalada barakeysan ee Maka iyo gobolka Madiina, iyo sidoo kale waxa ay ku tilmaantay weerarrada sii socda ee ka dhanka ah Boqortooyada Sacuudi Carabiya. OIC ayaa sheegtay in weerarradaasi ay cabsi ku abuureen shacabka rayidka ah, isla markaana ay xadgudub ku yihiin xurmada goobaha barakeysan iyo masaajidda, taas oo ay tilmaantay inay dhaawacayso dareenka Muslimiinta dunida. Ururku wuxuu sidoo kale sheegay in falalka ay ku tilmaantay kuwo ay geysteen Xuutiyiintu oo lagu beegsaday goobaha barakeysan, masaajidda iyo kaabayaasha rayidka ay yihiin falal argagixisanimo oo ka hor imanaya qiyamka Islaamka iyo xeerarka, mabaadi’da iyo shuruucda caalamiga ah. Xoghaynta Guud ee OIC waxay carrabka ku adkaysay in xadgudub kasta oo lagu sameeyo xurmada goobaha barakeysan uu yahay arrin aan la aqbali karin, iyadoo ku baaqday in laga hortago cid kasta oo isku dayda inay waxyeello u geysato goobahaas. Dhanka kale, OIC waxay sheegtay inay si buuxda u garab taagan tahay Boqortooyada Sacuudi Carabiya, ayna taageersan tahay tallaabooyinka ay Riyadh qaaddo si ay uga hortagto weerarrada, u ilaaliso xurmada goobaha barakeysan iyo nolosha Muslimiinta, isla markaana ay u difaacdo amniga iyo madaxbannaanida dalka.

items.title: Cali Cosoble oo ka digay qorshe ay damacsan yihiin Dabageed iyo Sanabloolshe
items.description: Muqdisho (Caasimada Online) – Madaxweynihii hore ee HirSHabelle, Cali Cabdullahi Cosoble oo qoraal soo saaray ayaa ka digay dhaq-dhaqaaqyada ka socda Beledweyne, isaga oo si gaar ah ugu eedeeyay madaxweyne ku xigeenka HirShabelle Yuusuf Dabageed iyo taliyihii hore ee NISA Cabdullahi Maxamed Cali (Sanbaloolshe) oo ku sugan magaaladaas oo xarun u ah Hiiraan. Cali Cosoble ayaa ku eedeeyay Dabageed iyo Sanbaloolshe in markii ay Madaxweyne Xasan Sheekh Maxamuud ka waayeen wixii ay raadinayeen ay u dhaqaaqeen Beledweyne, si ay halkaas uga raadiyaan danahooda siyaasadeed, isaga oo sidoo kale ku baaqay in aan loo ogolaan inay dagaan xarunta gobolka. “Qorshaha Dabageed iyo Sanbaloolshe waa wixii ay Xasan Sheekh ka wayeen ayey B/weyne ka soo raadiyeen. Ujeedo kale ma laha ee yaan laga aqbalin iney xaunta gobolka dhax dagaan. Waxaad moodaa inuu Dabaged rabo inuu Cali Madaxweyne isku dilo,” ayuu yiri madaxweynihii hore ee HirShabelle. Waxaa kale oo uu sii raaciyay “Cali Madaxweyne waxgaradkiisa waxaan kula talinayaa iney Dabageed ka saaraan xarunta gobolka. Beledweyne waa weyn tahay ee meeshii kale oo uu rabo ha ka dago laakin xarunta waa maya”. Cosoble oo hadalkiisa sii wata ayaa sheegay in ujeeddada siyaasiyiintan ay tahay inay fowdo ka abuuraan Beledweyne, isla markaana ay fursad siyaasadeed ka dhex raadinayaan shacabka Hiiraan oo uu sheegay inay horay u dayaceen. Waxaa kale oo uu tilmaamay in siyaasiyiinta ay doonayaan in gobolka ay ka abuuraan xaalad qalqal iyo khilaaf ah, si ay Madaxweyne Xasan Sheekh Maxamuud ugu muujiyaan inay weli awood ku leeyihiin gobolka Hiiraan. “Dabageed madaxweyne ku xigeenkii ayuu soo waayay ee yuusan idiin seex-seexan. Halka uu Sanbaloolshe Xasan Sheekh u diiday inuu Hirshabelle madaxweyne ka noqdo. Labadooda markey caariyeen wexey u soo jeesteen iney gobolka fowdo ka kiciyaan si ay Xasan Sheekh u tusaan iney labadooda heystaan Hiiraan. Yaan la aqbalin owr kacsiga nimanka ilma adeerka ah ee isku ujeedadana ah. items.description: Washington, DC The Somaliland President, Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi, met with members of both Houses of the United States Congress and members of the Diplomatic Corps for brunch. items.description: Madaxweynaha Jamhuuriyadda Somaliland, Mudane Cabdiraxmaan Maxamed Cabdillaahi (Cirro), ayaa maanta booqday Xarunta Congress-ka Maraykanka (United States Capitol Hill) oo ah goobta ay ku shaqeeyaan Xildhibaannada Aqalka Sare (Senate) iyo kuwa Golaha Wakiillada (House of Representatives), halkaas oo uu kulamo muhiim ah kula yeeshay xubno ka tirsan Congress-ka Maraykanka, oo ay ka mid yihiin Xildhibaan (Congressman) John Rose (R-Tennessee) iyo Xildhibaan (Congressman) John Moolenaar (R-Michigan). Madaxweynaha iyo xubnaha Congress-ka ayaa si qoto dheer uga wada hadlay xoojinta iskaashiga Somaliland iyo Maraykanka, iyaga oo si gaar ah u taabtay arrimaha amniga, iskaashiga istiraatiijiga ah, ganacsiga, maalgashiga iyo xasilloonida Gobolka Geeska Afrika. Madaxweynaha Jamhuuriyadda Somaliland ayaa adkeeyey muhimadda ay Somaliland u leedahay amniga iyo xasilloonida Geeska Afrika, Gacanka Cadmeed iyo Badda Cas, isaga oo tilmaamay in juqraafi ahaan Somaliland ay ku taallo meel muhiim u ah ilaalinta marinnada ganacsiga caalamiga ah iyo danaha istiraatiijiga ah ee muhiimka u ah dalka Maraykanka. Sida oo kale, Madaxweynaha Jamhuuriyadda Somaliland ayaa carrabka ku adkeeyey in Somaliland doonayso iskaashi ku salaysan dano-wadaag, masuuliyad iyo natiijooyin la taaban karo, gaar ahaan horumarinta iskaashiga amni, ballaadhinta ganacsiga, dhiirrigelinta maalgashiga Maraykanka iyo xoojinta xidhiidhada dhaqaale.

items.title: NISA oo qabatay Shabaab lagu diyaariyay Muqdisho
items.description: Muqdisho (Caasimada Online) – Taliska Hay’adda Nabadsugidda Qaranka ayaa faah-faahin ka bixiyay howlgal lagu burburiyay shabakado ka tirsan kooxda Al-Shabaab oo loo diyaariyay inay ka howlgaan magaalada Muqdisho. Warsaxaafadeed kasoo baxa NISA ayaa lagu sheegay in shabakadahan qorshahooda la fashiliyay ujeedkooda uu ahaan inay ku dhex dhuuntaan shacabka caasimada, kadibna ay sidaas ku fuliyaan qaraxyo iyo dilal qorsheysan. Inta uu socday howlgalka waxaa sidoo kale gacanta lagu soo dhigay illaa 11 xubnood oo ka tirsanaa shabakadaha la burburiyay, sida lagu sheegay qoraalka. “Ciidanka Hay’adda Sirdoonka iyo Nabadsugidda Qaranka (NISA) ayaa burburiyay shabakado ka tirsan Khawaarijta, kuwaas oo cadawgu u diyaariyay in ay ku dhex dhuuntaan qaybo ka mid ah caasimadda Muqdisho iyo nawaaxigeeda, waxaana gacanta lagu dhigay 11 dhagar-qabe oo ka tirsanaa shabakado kala duwan, kuwaas oo loo diyaarinayay in ay fuliyaan falal ka dhan ah amniga,” ayaa lagu yiri warsaxaafadeedka kasoo baxay taliska NISA. Sidoo kale howlgalladan oo ka dhacay 5 degmo oo kala duwan ayaa lagu soo qabtay hub iyo agabyo kale oo ay lahaayeen maleeshiyaadka Al-Shabaab. “Shabakadahaan ayaa la soo afjaray kaddib howlgallo qorsheysan oo Ciidanka NISA ay ka fuliyeen degmooyinka Daarusalaam, Garasbaaley, Kaxda, Dayniile iyo Afgooye. Intii ay howlgalladu socdeen, ciidamada ayaa sidoo kale gacanta ku dhigay hub iyo agab kale oo ay dhagar-qabayaashu doonayeen in ay u adeegsadaan fulinta dhagarta ay qorsheynayeen,” ayaa lasii raaciyay qoraalka. Howlgalladan ayaa qayb ka ah dadaallada joogtada ah ee ay taliska NISA uga hortagayso qorshayaasha ay maleeshiyaadka Al-Shabaab ku doonayaan inay ku waxyeelleeyaan amniga iyo shacabka Soomaaliyeed. “Muwaadin, wixii khatar amni ah ama macluumaad la xiriira Khawaarijta Al-Shabaab iyo Daacish, la wadaag NISA: 199 | 0770 747474 | 0620 545454,” ayaa lagu soo gabagabeeyay bayaanka Hay’adda Nabadsugidda Soomaaliya. Magaalada Muqdisho ayaa haatan ah mid aad u xasilloon, iyadoo ay meesha ka baxeen qaraxyadii iyo weerarradii ay horay argagixisadu uga gaysan jirtay caasimada. Xasilloonidan ayaa loo aaneynayaa dadaallada dowladda ee lagu xoojinayo sugidda amniga, kadib markii ciidamada amniga si wanaagsan loo jiheeyay, loona kordhiyay howlgallada lagu xaqiijinayo nabadgelyada guud. The post NISA oo qabatay Shabaab lagu diyaariyay Muqdisho appeared first on Caasimada Online .

items.title: Safiirka Suudaan oo la arkay isagoo kaligiis dhex socda Muqdisho + Video
items.description: Muqdisho (Caasimada Online) – Safiirka Suudaan u qaabilsan arrimaha Soomaaliya, Mudane Cabdulraxmaan Khaliil Axmed ayaa maanta qaaday tallaabo hadal-heyn dhalisay, kadib markii la arkay, isagoo kaligiis dhex socda mid kamid ah waddooyinka magaalada Muqdisho ee caasimada dalka. Muuqaalka safiirka Suudaan ee Soomaaliya ayaa si weyn ugu baahay baraha bulshada, isagoo hor taagan maqaayad ay Muqdisho ku leeyihiin muwaadiniin Suudaanees ah, waxaana muuqda hal gaari iyo darawalka safiirka oo kaliya. Danjiraha ayaa sidoo kale dalab ka qaatay maqaayadda, isagoo ganacsatada reer Suudaan ee uu la kulmay ku dhiirageliyay ganacsigooda. Tallaabada safiirka Suudaan ayaa lagu tilmaamay mid xujo ku ah siyaasiyiinta iyo diblumaasiyiinta wata gawaarida iyo askarta faraha badan ee hubeysan, kuwaas oo muujinayo in weli khatar amni ay ka jirto magaalada Muqdisho. Arrintan ayaa sidoo kale muujineysa amniga wanaagsan ee haatan ka jira caasimada dalka, kaas oo wax badan laga qabtay sanadihii ugu dambeeyay. Haddaba sidee looga fal-celiyay tallaabada safiirka Suudaan? Qaar kamid ah dadweynaha isticmaala baraha bulshada ayaa si weyn uga fal-celiyay arrinta cajiibka ah ee uu sameeyay Danjire Cabdulraxmaan Khaliil Axmed, maadaama uu diray farriin cad oo la xiriirta amniga ka jira Muqdisho. Dadka ka fal-celiyay muuqaalka ayaa sheegay in aysan suuragal ahayn in safiir ka yimid dal kale uu sidaan ugu kalsoonaado amniga magaalada Muqdisho, halka weli siyaasiyiinta dalka ay wataan gaadiid iyo askar badan. Cabdixayi Shaafi: “Waa tallaabo wanaagsan oo tusinaysa amniga ay caasimadu ku talaabsatay, lkn waxaa wax laga xumado ah in siyaasiyiinta Soomaalidu ay ka xunyihiin amniga dalka”. Ayuub Maxamuud: “Suudaaniyiiinta allaha sharfo waa dad qiimo badan wax weyna inaga dhexeeyaan”. Cabdiraxmaan Muumin: “Sida ay u faraxsan yihiin m.a aad iyo aad ayey u jecel yihiin Soomaalida waa karaameeyaan”. The post Safiirka Suudaan oo la arkay isagoo kaligiis dhex socda Muqdisho + Video appeared first on Caasimada Online .

items.title: NISA oo Muqdisho iyo nawaaxigeeda ku qabatay 11 xubnood oo lagu eedeeyay inay ka tirsanaayeen Shabaab
items.description: Muqdisho, 15 Sebteembar 2026 — Hay’adda Sirdoonka iyo Nabadsugidda Qaranka (NISA) ayaa sheegtay inay burburisay shabakado ay ku eedeysay inay ka tirsanaayeen Shabaab kuwaas oo la sheegay in loo diyaariyay inay si qarsoodi ah uga howlgalaan qaybo ka mid ah Muqdisho iyo nawaaxigeeda. Sida lagu sheegay war kasoo baxay NISA, ciidamada ayaa howlgallo qorsheysan ka sameeyay Daarusalaam, Garasbaaley, Kaxda, Dayniile iyo Afgooye, iyadoo intii ay socdeen lagu qabtay 11 qof oo lagu tilmaamay inay ka tirsanaayeen shabakado kala duwan. Hay’addu waxay sheegtay in dadka la qabtay loo diyaarinayay fulinta falal ay ku waxyeelleyn lahaayeen amniga iyo shacabka Soomaaliyeed. Sidoo kale, howlgalada ayaa lagu qabtay hub iyo agab kale, kuwaas oo sida NISA sheegtay loo adeegsan lahaa fulinta qorshayaal amni-darro. NISA ayaa sheegtay in howlgaladani ay qayb ka yihiin dadaallada joogtada ah ee hay’addu ku xoojinayso amniga caasimadda iyo ka hortagga qorshayaasha kooxaha hubeysan.

items.title: Op-ed: What Somalia Can Learn from Singapore
items.description: By Mohamed Hared Mohamed; This personal reflection by Mohamed Hared Mohamed, who recently joined a delegation on a benchmarking visit to Singapore, explores the lessons Somalia can draw from Singapore’s experience in leadership, institutional development, public-sector transformation, and long-term national planning. Drawing on the August 2026 NLA/OPM Executive Leadership Study Tour to Singapore, the reflection considers how Singapore’s emphasis on discipline, human capital, digital transformation, merit, lifelong learning, infrastructure and institutional capacity can inform Somalia’s development journey. It argues that Somalia should not attempt to replicate Singapore’s institutions or circumstances, but should adapt relevant principles to its own political, social, economic and demographic realities. Attention is given to strengthening leadership development, professional public administration, youth investment, trade and logistics, green urban development, digital governance/gov-tech and diaspora engagement. The central message is that sustainable national transformation depends on turning ambition into capable institutions, effective systems and a culture of collective responsibility. Singapore leadership study tour delegates at Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy A Personal Reflection from the NLA/OPM Executive Leadership Study Tour There are journeys that take you to a place, and there are journeys that change the way you see your own country. My recent visit to Singapore with colleagues from the National Leadership Academy (NLA) of Somalia and Office of the Prime Minister, as part of an Executive Leadership Study Tour to the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy at the National University of Singapore, was very much the latter. Singapore was not simply impressive because of its skyscrapers, clean streets, efficient transport or spectacular architecture. What struck me most was the system behind the spectacle. Everywhere we went, from Changi Airport to the National University of Singapore, from Gardens by the Bay to the public transport network, from the historical quarters to the shopping districts, there appeared to be an underlying culture of planning, discipline, service excellence, accountability and continuous improvement. For the NLA delegation, the visit was particularly meaningful because our institutional mandate is itself centred on leadership development, public-sector capacity building, governance and the creation of a new generation of principled and capable Somali leaders. The study tour therefore became more than an academic visit. It became an opportunity to ask a difficult but necessary question: What can Somalia realistically learn from Singapore not by copying Singapore, but by understanding the principles that enabled Singapore to transform itself? The answer is not that Somalia should become Singapore. Somalia has its own history, geography, culture, institutions and realities. The lesson is that development is ultimately a product of choices, institutions, leadership, discipline and collective commitment. From Mogadishu to Singapore: The First Lesson Was at the Airport Our journey itself provided an interesting introduction to the contrast between different systems. Travelling from Somalia through Addis Ababa and onward to Singapore, we experienced a highly coordinated international travel system. Prior to arrival, travellers are required to complete the SG Arrival Card electronically within three days before arrival, an example of how digital systems can simplify and organise government processes before a citizen or visitor even reaches a physical government counter. ( ICA ) Upon arrival at Changi Airport, the experience was striking. Immigration processing relied heavily on digital technologies and automated clearance, creating an impression that government had been deliberately designed around efficiency and the user experience. For a Somali visitor, this creates an important reflection especially after several immigration stamping checks from the port of exit, Aden Adde International Airport. We often speak about digital transformation as if it means purchasing computers, developing websites or introducing software. Singapore demonstrates that digital transformation is fundamentally about redesigning processes. The question Somalia should therefore ask is not merely, “What technology can we buy?” but rather: “How can we redesign government services so that citizens experience government as simple, predictable, transparent and efficient?”, that is a leadership question before it is a technological question.   Singapore Is Small in Geography but Large in Ambition Singapore’s physical circumstances make its transformation even more remarkable. The country’s land area is approximately 744.3 square kilometres , according to Singapore’s official statistics. ( SingStat ) Yet within that limited physical space, Singapore has developed a globally connected economy, sophisticated infrastructure, strong institutions, advanced education systems and a highly organised urban environment. Its population stood at 6.11 million in June 2025 comprising of 3.66 million citizens, 0.54 million permanent residents and 1.91 million non-residents. ( Population Singapore ) The lesson here is not about geographical size. It is about how a country converts constraints into incentives for innovation , with its limited space Singapore had to plan its land carefully, lacking natural resources but rather heavily investing in human capital thus aiding them to compete internationally using sporadically magnificent measures in place that built connectivity, infrastructure and institutions capable of attracting investment and talent. For Somalia, the lesson is equally powerful as it possesses assets Singapore did not have in abundance: a long coastline, agricultural potential, livestock, fisheries, a young population, strategic proximity to the Gulf, the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean and a globally dispersed diaspora. The question is therefore not whether Somalia has potential, but can it develop the institutions and leadership discipline necessary to convert potential into national prosperity. The Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy: Leadership as an Institution Our central purpose in Singapore was the Executive Leadership Study Tour at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy and engagements across the National University of Singapore ecosystem. The programme exposed the NLA/OPM team to approaches on executive education, public-sector leadership, lifelong learning, digital education and institutional development. We also engaged with institutions including the Institute for Adult Learning (IAL), NUS Institute of Systems Science/Digital Academy, and NUS School of Continuing and Lifelong Education (SCALE) at Kent Ridge, while experiencing the broader University Town campus and lifelong-learning environment. A formidable lesson from the Singapore experience is that leadership development cannot be reduced to occasional workshops, because its sine qua non to have an institutional ecosystem that connects executive education, public-sector training, evidence and research, policy analysis, digital learning, professional development, case-based learning, continuous learning and sustained engagement with government and society. This has direct relevance for the National Leadership Academy (NLA), which has an opportunity to evolve beyond being merely a leadership training centre into a national platform for leadership knowledge, executive education, public-sector transformation, research and policy dialogue. Such an institution would develop leaders not only through theoretical instruction but by engaging them with real governance challenges, generating evidence, translating research into policy and creating continuous opportunities for professional learning and reflection. As McDougal, Lasswell and Reisman (1973) aptly observed, “Intelligence is a critical function at all levels of decision making, yet its very ubiquity seems to have obscured it from visibility to scholarly inquiry.” This insight reinforces the need for NLA to position leadership intelligence, evidence-informed decision-making and policy learning at the heart of Somalia’s public-sector leadership and institutional transformation agenda.   From Meritocracy to Competence: The Leadership Question Singapore’s experience also raises an important conversation around meritocracy. Having previously engaged with publications examining Singapore’s evolving meritocracy, I arrived with an academic interest in the subject but left with a more practical reflection, institutions perform better when competence, responsibility and performance matter. This doesn’t mean that Somalia should mechanically reproduce Singapore’s model for our social and political context is fundamentally different, but the underlying principle deserves attention. A functioning state needs systems that identify capable people, develop them, place them where they can contribute, evaluate their performance and continuously build their competencies. For Somalia, this means that there is need to strengthen merit, professional development, performance management and institutional accountability to transform the vital aspect of leadership leveraging the world’s youngest populations as the country’s demographic reality means leadership development can never be postponed. The challenge isn’t simply to find young people jobs but rather prepare young Somalis to become competent administrators, entrepreneurs, researchers, diplomats, engineers, policy specialists, educators and public leaders. That is precisely where institutions such as NLA can play a transformative role. A Young Somalia and an Ageing Singapore: Two Very Different Demographic Challenges One of the most striking contrasts between Somalia and Singapore is demographics as the latter’s total fertility rate was 0.97 in 2024 , while its total population was 6.11 million in June 2025. ( Population Singapore ) contrastingly, Somalia has a very young population and a substantially higher fertility rate hence two different national challenges for two different countries world apart. Singapore is asking: How do we encourage families to have children and ensure that future generations are adequately supported? On our arrival date to Singapore, Sunday, 23 August 2026 there was National Day Rally, where Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced expanded support for families, with children expected to receive almost S$70,000 in direct financial support as they grow up, alongside childcare, education and other family-support measures. ( Prime Minister’s Office Singapore ) Somalia faces almost the opposite challenge: How do we convert a very large youth population into an economic and demographic dividend? This is where Somalia’s greatest opportunity may lie. A young population without education, skills and employment can become a source of frustration but a young population equipped with skills, entrepreneurship, technology and ethical leadership can become the country’s greatest national asset. The Key takeaway lesson herein isn’t to copy Singapore’s population policy but rather to recognise the importance of anticipating demographic realities and building institutions around them. For Somalia, that means investing now in the human capital of its young population. The Singapore Civil Service: Government as One System Another powerful lesson concerns public-sector coordination. Singapore’s approach demonstrates the value of viewing government as an interconnected system rather than a collection of isolated ministries. For Somalia, one area worth exploring is a structured civil-service rotational and secondment programme since a carefully designed system could allow selected civil servants to undertake temporary assignments across federal ministries, Federal Member States and public institutions. Such exposure could help officials understand different sectors, strengthen coordination and build a generation of public servants capable of seeing government from a whole-of-government perspective (WOG). The objective wouldn’t be to copy Singapore’s system wholesale rather Somalia could adapt the principle of cross-government learning and professional mobility to its own federal context. A pilot could begin with senior and mid-level civil servants with clear rules around grade, tenure, benefits, professional development and performance such an approach could help reduce institutional silos and strengthen the culture of government as a shared national enterprise.     Trade: Somalia Should Look at Its Coast Differently Perhaps one of the most consequential lessons from Singapore concerns economic geography for it didn’t simply become successful because it manufactured goods. Its transformation involved the deliberate development of a high-value, trade-oriented economy built around connectivity, logistics, human capital and services. For Somalia, this is particularly relevant with a strategic coastline sitting close to some of the world’s most important maritime and commercial routes as geography alone doesn’t generate prosperity but rather Infrastructure, customs systems, security, skills, ports, financial services, logistics and predictable regulation are what turn geography into economic value. Somalia therefore has an opportunity to develop what might be described as a: “Singapore model adapted to the Somali coast.” This could mean: a multifaceted approach with efficient ports, reliable customs, digital trade systems, skilled young people, logistics, private investment and regional connectivity thus making Mogadishu, Kismayo and other Somali ports superior revenue generating beacons that mould gateways connecting East Africa, the Gulf and Asia hence making Somalia a regional economic giant. With reference to Singapore’s entrepôt trading system, Somalia has a potential to become a place where goods are transported, stored, processed, packaged, financed and re-exported. This requires patient institution-building, but the economic opportunity is enormous. From Gardens to Green Cities: When Green Development Becomes National Identity Our visit to Gardens by the Bay, Singapore Botanic Gardens, Sentosa Island and the entire smart green city demonstrated how Singapore has transformed green spaces, public institutions, tourism and urban planning into components of national development and identity. Somalia has the foundations of a similar opportunity in places such as Peace Garden, Darusalam Garden and Jazeera Aqua Park among others in Mogadishu for instance but bringing these spaces to Singapore’s level would require substantial investment in planning, maintenance, landscaping, water management, accessibility and public-private partnerships. The lesson, however, is not to reproduce Singapore physically but to borrow its philosophy of turning public spaces into assets for education, tourism, recreation, environmental resilience and economic development. Somalia could gradually transform its gardens, parks, beaches and coastal spaces into well-planned green and recreational destinations while integrating trees, water conservation, renewable energy, waste management and climate-resilient design into urban development. In this sense, Singapore offers Somalia a powerful reminder that a garden is not merely a garden it can become an investment in the environment, the economy, public wellbeing and national identity.     Cleanliness, Discipline and the Social Contract Perhaps one of the most memorable aspects of Singapore wasn’t its under-ground malls or technology but the behaviour of all and sundry in that city wasn’t something that goes without saying, clean streets, orderly public spaces, disciplined traffic, organised queues, respect for designated areas and a general sense that public spaces belong to everyone created a powerful social environment. During the visit, I was particularly struck by Singapore’s approach to smoking and vaping. Smoking is prohibited in numerous public places, while designated smoking areas are provided in permitted locations. ( National Environment Agency ). Singapore also maintains strict controls on vaping; possession and use of vaporisers are prohibited under its current regulatory framework. ( gov.sg ) Chewing gum is also among goods prohibited for import, subject to specified exceptions. ( Singapore Customs ) The lesson is not that Somalia should copy every Singaporean restriction but how can our people come together and commit to this kind of social contract. Rules work when citizens understand that individual behaviour affects the collective environment and when institutions consistently enforce reasonable rules. Development therefore requires both strong institutions and responsible citizens since one sustainably can’t exist without the other in line with the nature of the Triple Bottom Line. Transport: Mobility as an Economic System Singapore’s transport network offered another lesson in integrated planning with the experience of travelling around the city through buses, cable cars, trains, underground connections and integrated commercial spaces demonstrating that transport isn’t merely about moving people from one location to another. It’s about the way it connects people to education, employment, commerce, housing and recreation. Singapore’s Land Transport Authority describes integrated transport hubs where bus interchanges connect directly with MRT stations and adjoining developments such as shopping centres. ( Land Transport Authority ) Conversely for Somalia, transport infrastructure should similarly be viewed as part of economic development because a reliable public transport can connect young people to universities, workers to employment, businesses to markets and communities to essential services. The result is to Build an integrated mobility system that supports economic and social opportunity. The Other Singapore: Heritage, Identity and Cultural Confidence Singapore is sometimes presented exclusively as a modern city of glass towers and technology contrastingly we saw a distinct city walking through The Arab Street, Sultan Mosque, Little India and the Malay Heritage Centre demonstrated that modernization does not necessarily require the disappearance of history. The coexistence of modern commercial districts with religious, cultural and historical spaces provides an important undertaking for Somalia to curb chances of cultural amnesia with an efficient utilization of the extraordinary cultural and historical inheritance from Islamic scholarship and architecture to coastal trading history, oral traditions, poetry and diverse local cultures, the country can build modern cities while preserving and celebrating its identity. It’s important to note that cultural preservation is surely an economic and diplomatic asset through heritage tourism, museums, cultural institutions, research and creative industries. What Somalia Should Borrow and What It Should Not The central lesson Somalia can draw from Singapore is not to reproduce its institutions wholesale, but to understand the principles behind them and adapt them to Somalia’s own political, economic and social realities. Singapore’s experience shows the value of long-term planning, competent public administration, investment in human capital, digital government, integrated infrastructure, trade and logistics, environmental planning and life-long education. At the same time, the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy’s work on Singapore’s Evolving Meritocracy demonstrates that even successful systems must continually reassess themselves, particularly when meritocracy risks becoming associated with privilege or narrow definitions of academic success. For Somalia, the lesson is therefore to build institutions that reward competence, integrity, skills and performance while ensuring that opportunities are accessible beyond established networks. ( Singapore’s Evolving Meritrocracy ) Somalia should also learn from Singapore’s ability to respond pragmatically to economic shocks. The LKYSPP case study on Singapore’s Approach to Managing Economic Crises shows that Singapore responded to crises through coordinated fiscal, monetary and institutional measures designed to protect employment, reduce pressure on businesses and stimulate recovery. The important lesson for Somalia is not to replicate Singapore’s specific financial instruments, which depend on a very different fiscal and institutional environment, but to develop its own crisis-management capacity: credible public institutions, reliable economic data, contingency planning, social protection mechanisms and the ability to coordinate government and private-sector responses when shocks occur. ( Singapore’s Approach to Managing Economic Crises ) The issue of migration provides another important lesson. Singapore has used migration as part of its economic strategy, but its experience also demonstrates the difficult balance between economic needs, national interests and the rights of migrants. The LKYSPP’s Ethics of Migration highlights the competing interests of governments, citizens, employers, migrant workers and countries of origin. For Somalia, this is particularly relevant because the country has both a large diaspora and significant outward migration. Somalia can therefore move beyond viewing migration primarily as a problem and develop a national migration and diaspora strategy that connects Somali professionals abroad with investment, skills transfer, research, entrepreneurship and public-sector development, while also strengthening protections and opportunities for Somalis who migrate. ( The Ethics of Migration ) What This Means for the National Leadership Academy For the National Leadership Academy (NLA) , the Singapore experience has surely become more of an institutional learning agenda rather than a study tour. As we aim to gradually strengthen executive education and leadership programmes that are public-sector centric with focus on strategic management, digital governance, policy analysis, institutional performance and lifelong learning while utilizing comparative cases such as Singapore to ask a more important question: what can realistically work in Somalia? This approach is consistent with the broader direction of the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy where policy education connects research, professional learning and real-world governance challenges. NLA’s Research and Innovation Centre looks forward to turn international experiences into locally grounded research on peace ,security, migration, climate resilience and public-sector transformation. ( Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy ) The National Leadership Academy also hopes to serve as a bridge between Somalia and its global knowledge networks. Somalia’s diaspora contains professionals working across government, academia, technology, finance, medicine, engineering, diplomacy, business and international development. Rather than treating this expertise as an informal resource, NLA has created structured mechanisms for mentorship, visiting expertise, executive education, policy dialogue and knowledge transfer. Singapore’s experience suggests that national development depends not only on possessing talented people but on creating institutions capable of organising that talent around national priorities. For Somalia, this could become one of NLA’s most practical contributions to institution-building. The Hardest Lesson: Singapore Did Not Become Singapore Overnight Perhaps the most important lesson is that Singapore’s transformation was not the product of one leader, one policy or one institution. It emerged through decades of institution-building, policy continuity, human-capital investment, infrastructure development and adaptation. Even Singapore’s own experience shows that successful systems must evolve; the LKYSPP’s discussion of meritocracy, for example, recognises that a system initially built around ability and performance can face new questions about inequality, privilege and how merit should be defined. ( Singapore’s Evolving Meritrocracy ) Somalia should therefore avoid the attractive but misleading question, “How can one leader make Somalia like Singapore?” The more useful question is how Somalia can build institutions and a social compact capable of sustaining reform across governments, political cycles and generations. From Singapore to Somalia: The Journey Home Our five-day experience in Singapore therefore leaves us with questions rather than simple answers: How can NLA strengthen executive education? How can Somalia develop a more professional civil service? How can its ports become engines of trade? How can its young population become an economic dividend? How can climate resilience become part of urban planning? How can digital government become a functioning reality? And how can institutions become stronger than individual personalities? These questions extend beyond NLA, but the Academy will surely provide a national platform where public servants, researchers, academics, private-sector actors and diaspora professionals examine international experience and translate relevant lessons into Somali policy and practice. Conclusion: Singapore as Inspiration, Somalia as the Mission In a nutshell, my strongest reflection from Singapore is that the country’s greatest achievement is not its skyline, gardens, transport system or architecture, impressive as all of these are. It is the system behind them: planning, institutional capacity, public administration, human-capital development, continuous adaptation and collective responsibility. Singapore’s response to economic crises demonstrates the value of institutional preparedness; its evolving meritocracy demonstrates that even successful systems must continually examine themselves; and its migration experience illustrates the importance of balancing economic objectives with social and ethical considerations. Somalia therefore does not need to become Singapore. It needs to become the best version of Somalia. Its young population, strategic coastline, natural resources, entrepreneurial culture, diaspora and human capital provide significant foundations, but these assets must be converted into functioning institutions and productive systems. The real lesson is therefore simple: Somalia should not copy Singapore’s destination; it should learn from the discipline of Singapore’s journey. If Somalia can build institutions that value competence, invest in its young people, embrace technology, strengthen public administration, develop its infrastructure, harness its diaspora and promote accountability, then it can create its own model of prosperity a peaceful, capable and globally connected Somalia rather than a Somali version of Singapore. The ultimate lesson for NLA is that ambition becomes transformative only when it is converted into institutions, institutions into systems and systems into a culture shared by society.   References: The National Population and Talent Division (NPTD) of Singapore: https://www.population.gov.sg/who-we-are/ The Office of the Prime Minister Singapore: National Day Rally, https://www.pmo.gov.sg/newsroom/ndr2026/ Dodgson, J., & Auyong, H. (2018). The Ethics of Migration . Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, National University of Singapore. The Ethics of Migration LKYSPP Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy. (2018). Singapore’s Approach to Managing Economic Crises . National University of Singapore. Singapore’s Approach to Managing Economic Crises LKYSPP PDF Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy. (2020). Singapore’s Evolving Meritocracy . National University of Singapore. Singapore’s Evolving Meritocracy LKYSPP PDF Immigration & Checkpoints Authority. (2026). For Somalia, this means that there is need to strengthen merit, professional development, performance management and institutional accountability to transform the vital aspect of leadership leveraging the world’s youngest populations as the country’s demographic reality means leadership development can never be postponed. The challenge isn’t simply to find young people jobs but rather prepare young Somalis to become competent administrators, entrepreneurs, researchers, diplomats, engineers, policy specialists, educators and public leaders. That is precisely where institutions such as NLA can play a transformative role. A Young Somalia and an Ageing Singapore: Two Very Different Demographic Challenges One of the most striking contrasts between Somalia and Singapore is demographics as the latter’s total fertility rate was 0.97 in 2024 , while its total population was 6.11 million in June 2025. ( Population Singapore ) contrastingly, Somalia has a very young population and a substantially higher fertility rate hence two different national challenges for two different countries world apart. Singapore is asking: How do we encourage families to have children and ensure that future generations are adequately supported? On our arrival date to Singapore, Sunday, 23 August 2026 there was National Day Rally, where Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced expanded support for families, with children expected to receive almost S$70,000 in direct financial support as they grow up, alongside childcare, education and other family-support measures. ( Prime Minister’s Office Singapore ) Somalia faces almost the opposite challenge: How do we convert a very large youth population into an economic and demographic dividend? This is where Somalia’s greatest opportunity may lie. A young population without education, skills and employment can become a source of frustration but a young population equipped with skills, entrepreneurship, technology and ethical leadership can become the country’s greatest national asset. The Key takeaway lesson herein isn’t to copy Singapore’s population policy but rather to recognise the importance of anticipating demographic realities and building institutions around them. For Somalia, that means investing now in the human capital of its young population. The Singapore Civil Service: Government as One System Another powerful lesson concerns public-sector coordination. Singapore’s approach demonstrates the value of viewing government as an interconnected system rather than a collection of isolated ministries. For Somalia, one area worth exploring is a structured civil-service rotational and secondment programme since a carefully designed system could allow selected civil servants to undertake temporary assignments across federal ministries, Federal Member States and public institutions. Such exposure could help officials understand different sectors, strengthen coordination and build a generation of public servants capable of seeing government from a whole-of-government perspective (WOG). The objective wouldn’t be to copy Singapore’s system wholesale rather Somalia could adapt the principle of cross-government learning and professional mobility to its own federal context. A pilot could begin with senior and mid-level civil servants with clear rules around grade, tenure, benefits, professional development and performance such an approach could help reduce institutional silos and strengthen the culture of government as a shared national enterprise.     Trade: Somalia Should Look at Its Coast Differently Perhaps one of the most consequential lessons from Singapore concerns economic geography for it didn’t simply become successful because it manufactured goods. Its transformation involved the deliberate development of a high-value, trade-oriented economy built around connectivity, logistics, human capital and services. For Somalia, this is particularly relevant with a strategic coastline sitting close to some of the world’s most important maritime and commercial routes as geography alone doesn’t generate prosperity but rather Infrastructure, customs systems, security, skills, ports, financial services, logistics and predictable regulation are what turn geography into economic value. Somalia therefore has an opportunity to develop what might be described as a: “Singapore model adapted to the Somali coast.” This could mean: a multifaceted approach with efficient ports, reliable customs, digital trade systems, skilled young people, logistics, private investment and regional connectivity thus making Mogadishu, Kismayo and other Somali ports superior revenue generating beacons that mould gateways connecting East Africa, the Gulf and Asia hence making Somalia a regional economic giant. With reference to Singapore’s entrepôt trading system, Somalia has a potential to become a place where goods are transported, stored, processed, packaged, financed and re-exported. This requires patient institution-building, but the economic opportunity is enormous. From Gardens to Green Cities: When Green Development Becomes National Identity Our visit to Gardens by the Bay, Singapore Botanic Gardens, Sentosa Island and the entire smart green city demonstrated how Singapore has transformed green spaces, public institutions, tourism and urban planning into components of national development and identity. Somalia has the foundations of a similar opportunity in places such as Peace Garden, Darusalam Garden and Jazeera Aqua Park among others in Mogadishu for instance but bringing these spaces to Singapore’s level would require substantial investment in planning, maintenance, landscaping, water management, accessibility and public-private partnerships. The lesson, however, is not to reproduce Singapore physically but to borrow its philosophy of turning public spaces into assets for education, tourism, recreation, environmental resilience and economic development. Somalia could gradually transform its gardens, parks, beaches and coastal spaces into well-planned green and recreational destinations while integrating trees, water conservation, renewable energy, waste management and climate-resilient design into urban development. In this sense, Singapore offers Somalia a powerful reminder that a garden is not merely a garden it can become an investment in the environment, the economy, public wellbeing and national identity.     Cleanliness, Discipline and the Social Contract Perhaps one of the most memorable aspects of Singapore wasn’t its under-ground malls or technology but the behaviour of all and sundry in that city wasn’t something that goes without saying, clean streets, orderly public spaces, disciplined traffic, organised queues, respect for designated areas and a general sense that public spaces belong to everyone created a powerful social environment. During the visit, I was particularly struck by Singapore’s approach to smoking and vaping. Smoking is prohibited in numerous public places, while designated smoking areas are provided in permitted locations. ( National Environment Agency ). Singapore also maintains strict controls on vaping; possession and use of vaporisers are prohibited under its current regulatory framework. ( gov.sg ) Chewing gum is also among goods prohibited for import, subject to specified exceptions. ( Singapore Customs ) The lesson is not that Somalia should copy every Singaporean restriction but how can our people come together and commit to this kind of social contract. Rules work when citizens understand that individual behaviour affects the collective environment and when institutions consistently enforce reasonable rules. Development therefore requires both strong institutions and responsible citizens since one sustainably can’t exist without the other in line with the nature of the Triple Bottom Line. Transport: Mobility as an Economic System Singapore’s transport network offered another lesson in integrated planning with the experience of travelling around the city through buses, cable cars, trains, underground connections and integrated commercial spaces demonstrating that transport isn’t merely about moving people from one location to another. It’s about the way it connects people to education, employment, commerce, housing and recreation. Singapore’s Land Transport Authority describes integrated transport hubs where bus interchanges connect directly with MRT stations and adjoining developments such as shopping centres. ( Land Transport Authority ) Conversely for Somalia, transport infrastructure should similarly be viewed as part of economic development because a reliable public transport can connect young people to universities, workers to employment, businesses to markets and communities to essential services. The result is to Build an integrated mobility system that supports economic and social opportunity. The Other Singapore: Heritage, Identity and Cultural Confidence Singapore is sometimes presented exclusively as a modern city of glass towers and technology contrastingly we saw a distinct city walking through The Arab Street, Sultan Mosque, Little India and the Malay Heritage Centre demonstrated that modernization does not necessarily require the disappearance of history. The coexistence of modern commercial districts with religious, cultural and historical spaces provides an important undertaking for Somalia to curb chances of cultural amnesia with an efficient utilization of the extraordinary cultural and historical inheritance from Islamic scholarship and architecture to coastal trading history, oral traditions, poetry and diverse local cultures, the country can build modern cities while preserving and celebrating its identity. It’s important to note that cultural preservation is surely an economic and diplomatic asset through heritage tourism, museums, cultural institutions, research and creative industries. What Somalia Should Borrow and What It Should Not The central lesson Somalia can draw from Singapore is not to reproduce its institutions wholesale, but to understand the principles behind them and adapt them to Somalia’s own political, economic and social realities. Singapore’s experience shows the value of long-term planning, competent public administration, investment in human capital, digital government, integrated infrastructure, trade and logistics, environmental planning and life-long education. At the same time, the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy’s work on Singapore’s Evolving Meritocracy demonstrates that even successful systems must continually reassess themselves, particularly when meritocracy risks becoming associated with privilege or narrow definitions of academic success. For Somalia, the lesson is therefore to build institutions that reward competence, integrity, skills and performance while ensuring that opportunities are accessible beyond established networks. ( Singapore’s Evolving Meritrocracy ) Somalia should also learn from Singapore’s ability to respond pragmatically to economic shocks. The LKYSPP case study on Singapore’s Approach to Managing Economic Crises shows that Singapore responded to crises through coordinated fiscal, monetary and institutional measures designed to protect employment, reduce pressure on businesses and stimulate recovery. The important lesson for Somalia is not to replicate Singapore’s specific financial instruments, which depend on a very different fiscal and institutional environment, but to develop its own crisis-management capacity: credible public institutions, reliable economic data, contingency planning, social protection mechanisms and the ability to coordinate government and private-sector responses when shocks occur. ( Singapore’s Approach to Managing Economic Crises ) The issue of migration provides another important lesson. Singapore has used migration as part of its economic strategy, but its experience also demonstrates the difficult balance between economic needs, national interests and the rights of migrants. The LKYSPP’s Ethics of Migration highlights the competing interests of governments, citizens, employers, migrant workers and countries of origin. For Somalia, this is particularly relevant because the country has both a large diaspora and significant outward migration. Somalia can therefore move beyond viewing migration primarily as a problem and develop a national migration and diaspora strategy that connects Somali professionals abroad with investment, skills transfer, research, entrepreneurship and public-sector development, while also strengthening protections and opportunities for Somalis who migrate. ( The Ethics of Migration ) What This Means for the National Leadership Academy For the National Leadership Academy (NLA) , the Singapore experience has surely become more of an institutional learning agenda rather than a study tour. As we aim to gradually strengthen executive education and leadership programmes that are public-sector centric with focus on strategic management, digital governance, policy analysis, institutional performance and lifelong learning while utilizing comparative cases such as Singapore to ask a more important question: what can realistically work in Somalia? This approach is consistent with the broader direction of the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy where policy education connects research, professional learning and real-world governance challenges. NLA’s Research and Innovation Centre looks forward to turn international experiences into locally grounded research on peace ,security, migration, climate resilience and public-sector transformation. ( Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy ) The National Leadership Academy also hopes to serve as a bridge between Somalia and its global knowledge networks. Somalia’s diaspora contains professionals working across government, academia, technology, finance, medicine, engineering, diplomacy, business and international development. Rather than treating this expertise as an informal resource, NLA has created structured mechanisms for mentorship, visiting expertise, executive education, policy dialogue and knowledge transfer. Singapore’s experience suggests that national development depends not only on possessing talented people but on creating institutions capable of organising that talent around national priorities. For Somalia, this could become one of NLA’s most practical contributions to institution-building. The Hardest Lesson: Singapore Did Not Become Singapore Overnight Perhaps the most important lesson is that Singapore’s transformation was not the product of one leader, one policy or one institution. It emerged through decades of institution-building, policy continuity, human-capital investment, infrastructure development and adaptation. Even Singapore’s own experience shows that successful systems must evolve; the LKYSPP’s discussion of meritocracy, for example, recognises that a system initially built around ability and performance can face new questions about inequality, privilege and how merit should be defined. ( Singapore’s Evolving Meritrocracy ) Somalia should therefore avoid the attractive but misleading question, “How can one leader make Somalia like Singapore?” The more useful question is how Somalia can build institutions and a social compact capable of sustaining reform across governments, political cycles and generations. From Singapore to Somalia: The Journey Home Our five-day experience in Singapore therefore leaves us with questions rather than simple answers: How can NLA strengthen executive education? How can Somalia develop a more professional civil service? How can its ports become engines of trade? How can its young population become an economic dividend? How can climate resilience become part of urban planning? How can digital government become a functioning reality? And how can institutions become stronger than individual personalities? These questions extend beyond NLA, but the Academy will surely provide a national platform where public servants, researchers, academics, private-sector actors and diaspora professionals examine international experience and translate relevant lessons into Somali policy and practice. Conclusion: Singapore as Inspiration, Somalia as the Mission In a nutshell, my strongest reflection from Singapore is that the country’s greatest achievement is not its skyline, gardens, transport system or architecture, impressive as all of these are. It is the system behind them: planning, institutional capacity, public administration, human-capital development, continuous adaptation and collective responsibility. Singapore’s response to economic crises demonstrates the value of institutional preparedness; its evolving meritocracy demonstrates that even successful systems must continually examine themselves; and its migration experience illustrates the importance of balancing economic objectives with social and ethical considerations. Somalia therefore does not need to become Singapore. It needs to become the best version of Somalia. Its young population, strategic coastline, natural resources, entrepreneurial culture, diaspora and human capital provide significant foundations, but these assets must be converted into functioning institutions and productive systems. The real lesson is therefore simple: Somalia should not copy Singapore’s destination; it should learn from the discipline of Singapore’s journey. If Somalia can build institutions that value competence, invest in its young people, embrace technology, strengthen public administration, develop its infrastructure, harness its diaspora and promote accountability, then it can create its own model of prosperity a peaceful, capable and globally connected Somalia rather than a Somali version of Singapore. The ultimate lesson for NLA is that ambition becomes transformative only when it is converted into institutions, institutions into systems and systems into a culture shared by society.   References: The National Population and Talent Division (NPTD) of Singapore: https://www.population.gov.sg/who-we-are/ The Office of the Prime Minister Singapore: National Day Rally, https://www.pmo.gov.sg/newsroom/ndr2026/ Dodgson, J., & Auyong, H. items.title: Trump picks Devin Kennington as US ambassador to Somalia
items.description: Washington, United States — US President Donald Trump has nominated veteran diplomat Devin Kennington as the next US ambassador to Somalia, moving to fill a post that has been without a Senate-confirmed envoy since January. The White House announced the nomination on Monday, saying Kennington, of California, had been selected to serve as “Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the United States of America to the Federal Republic of Somalia”. His nomination was formally sent to the US Senate on September 14, along with a series of diplomatic and senior government appointments. The Senate must confirm Kennington before he can formally take up the post in Mogadishu. If confirmed, he would succeed Richard H. Riley, the last Senate-confirmed US ambassador to Somalia, whose posting ended earlier this year after the Trump administration recalled him as part of a wider reshuffle of American ambassadors. The administration ordered Riley’s recall in December 2025 , with his assignment due to conclude the following month. Riley, a career Foreign Service officer, had served as ambassador since 2024. He was sworn in on May 8 that year and later presented his credentials to President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud. Embassy transition Following Riley’s departure, Justin Davis took over as chargé d’affaires, becoming Washington’s most senior diplomat in Somalia while the ambassadorial post remained vacant. Davis led the US mission for nearly eight months before concluding his assignment in September. In a September 10 statement , the US Embassy in Mogadishu thanked Davis for his leadership in advancing US “counterterrorism, law enforcement, and immigration priorities”. The embassy simultaneously announced that Ruth Anne Stevens-Klitz would serve as the incoming chargé d’affaires, saying she would continue to advance the Trump administration’s “America First” priorities and strengthen US-Somalia relations. Stevens-Klitz is now leading the mission while Kennington’s nomination goes through the Senate confirmation process. Africa experience Kennington brings experience in African affairs from the US State Department. State Department records list him as the Great Lakes Unit Chief in the Bureau of African Affairs’ Office of Central African Affairs, where his portfolio covered US policy towards countries including the Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda and Burundi. He has also worked on the Democratic Republic of Congo portfolio, with US government records i dentifying him in senior roles dealing with the country. Kennington also has direct experience in the Horn of Africa from an earlier posting at the US Embassy in Djibouti, where he served in the consular section. The White House did not release a detailed biography alongside the nomination or indicate when the Senate may take it up. Security ties The nomination comes as security and counterterrorism remain at the centre of relations between Washington and Mogadishu. The United States is one of Somalia’s main security partners and continues to support Somali forces fighting Al-Shabaab and Islamic State militants. US Africa Command has also continued air strikes against militant targets in Somalia in coordination with the federal government. The change in diplomatic leadership comes during a period of broader political and security pressure in Somalia, including disputes over the country’s electoral process and continuing military operations against Al-Shabaab. Washington formally recognised Somalia’s federal government in 2013, more than two decades after the collapse of the central government in 1991. The United States re-established a permanent diplomatic presence in Mogadishu in December 2018, reopening its embassy after a 27-year absence. Kennington will remain ambassador-designate unless and until the Senate confirms his nomination. Stevens-Klitz will meanwhile continue to head the US mission in Mogadishu as chargé d’affaires. items.title: Ujeedka kulan Villa Somalia ku dhex-maray Xasan iyo safiirka Turkiga
items.description: Muqdsho (Caasimada Online) – Madaxweynaha Soomaaliya, Mudane Xasan Sheekh Maxamuud ayaa maanta Xarunta Madaxtooyada Qaranka ku qaabilay, Danjiraha Turkiga ee Soomaaliya Alper Aktaş, kaas oo soo gaba-gabeeyay howlgalkii diblumaasiyadeed ee dalka. Ujeedka kulanka ayaa ahaa mid sagootin ah, iyadoo Madaxweyne Xasan Sheekh uu Danjiraha uga mahadceliyay muddadii uu Soomaaliya ka soo shaqeeyay iyo dadaalladii uu ku bixiyay xoojinta xiriirka iyo iskaashiga ka dhexeeya Soomaaliya iyo Turkiga. Sidoo kale, Madaxweyne Xasan Sheekh ayaa u rajeeyay safiirka guul iyo horumar, maadaama uu soo gaba-gabeeyay howlihii diblomaasiyadeed ee uu dalka u joogay. Danjire Alper Aktaş ayaa isna Madaxweynaha uga mahadceliyay soo dhaweynta iyo sagootinta loo sameeyay, isagoo xusay muddadii uu Soomaaliya ka shaqeynayay iyo xiriirka dhow ee labada dal. Sagootinta Danjire Alper Aktaş ayaa kusoo beegmaysa xilli xiriirka Soomaaliya iyo Turkiga uu marayo heer sare, iyadoo labada dowladood ay sii wadaan dadaallada lagu ballaarinayo iskaashiga labada dhinac. Turkiga ayaa kamid ah dalalka xiriirka dhow la leh Soomaaliya, iyadoo labada dowladood ay iska kaashadaan dhinacyada amniga, dhaqaalaha, horumarinta iyo arrimo kale oo muhiim ah. Ankara ayaa sidoo kale door muuqda ka qaadatay taageerada Soomaaliya ee dhinacyada amniga iyo dhismaha hay’adaha dowladda, iyadoo labada dal ay sannadihii lasoo dhaafay xoojiyeen iskaashigooda istiraatiijiga ah. items.title: Bosaso Airport Becomes Latest Front in Mogadishu–Puntland Power Struggle
items.description: Bosaso (WDN) — The deepening political and security rift between Somalia’s Federal Government and Puntland has reached another sensitive flashpoint after Puntland authorities reportedly stopped several officials, including two federal military officers, from leaving Bosaso Airport for Mogadishu. The two officers were reportedly among federal personnel recently brought under the control of the Federal Government following developments in the Kuur-ilaalo area of Rako-Raaxo district. Also prevented from traveling was Abdulkadir Haji Abdullahi “Waraabe,” director of the orthopedic hospital in Carmo. Sultan Mahmoud Haji Abdullahi, a prominent traditional leader from Bari, was also briefly detained before being released. Following his release, the Sultan called for the immediate release of those still being held, arguing that the individuals were traveling for personal reasons and had a legitimate right to do so. “They were traveling for their own personal interests and have the right to travel,” the Sultan said. A Much Deeper Dispute The airport incident is more than an isolated confrontation. It reflects the increasingly troubled relationship between Mogadishu and Garowe over federal authority, security forces, elections and constitutional powers. The Federal Government has increasingly sought to expand its political and security presence across the country, presenting the effort as part of strengthening national institutions. Puntland, however, has repeatedly viewed such moves with suspicion, arguing that federal forces cannot simply deploy or move through Puntland without coordination with the state administration. At the heart of the dispute is a fundamental question: where does federal authority end, and where does the authority of a Federal Member State begin? Trust Is Running Out The most serious consequence of the confrontation is the erosion of trust. Political disagreements between Puntland and Mogadishu are not new, but disputes that were once largely political have increasingly entered the security sphere. The movement of soldiers, military equipment and government officials can now become a source of confrontation. Critics of President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s administration argue that Mogadishu is pursuing greater centralized control without first securing political consensus with the Federal Member States. They warn that expanding federal authority through security deployments rather than dialogue risks weakening, rather than strengthening, Somalia’s federal system. The absence of a clear public explanation from Puntland regarding the airport incident also leaves important questions unanswered. Nevertheless, the episode demonstrates how fragile relations have become. Bosaso as a Symbol Bosaso Airport has now become another visible symbol of Somalia’s unresolved federal crisis. What should have been a routine domestic journey instead became entangled in questions of political allegiance, security authority and competing jurisdictions. The larger danger is that continued confrontation could transform political mistrust into permanent institutional hostility. For Mogadishu, the message from Puntland should be clear: national authority cannot simply be asserted; it must be built through constitutional clarity, political dialogue and cooperation with the Federal Member States. For Puntland, however, the challenge is equally significant: responding to federal pressure without allowing political disagreements to develop into prolonged security confrontation. Until the two sides address the underlying dispute, incidents such as the one at Bosaso Airport are likely to remain symptoms of a much larger problem—the growing distance between Somalia’s Federal Government and one of its most politically assertive Federal Member States. Nevertheless, the episode demonstrates how fragile relations have become. Bosaso as a Symbol Bosaso Airport has now become another visible symbol of Somalia’s unresolved federal crisis. What should have been a routine domestic journey instead became entangled in questions of political allegiance, security authority and competing jurisdictions. The larger danger is that continued confrontation could transform political mistrust into permanent institutional hostility. For Mogadishu, the message from Puntland should be clear: national authority cannot simply be asserted; it must be built through constitutional clarity, political dialogue and cooperation with the Federal Member States. For Puntland, however, the challenge is equally significant: responding to federal pressure without allowing political disagreements to develop into prolonged security confrontation. Until the two sides address the underlying dispute, incidents such as the one at Bosaso Airport are likely to remain symptoms of a much larger problem—the growing distance between Somalia’s Federal Government and one of its most politically assertive Federal Member States. items.title: Somaliland and Puntland Build Cordial Ties Through Security and Trade Cooperation
items.description: Washington (WDN) — Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi Irro has highlighted what he described as a growing and constructive relationship between Somaliland and Puntland, emphasizing dialogue, security cooperation and easier movement of people and goods between the two neighboring administrations. Speaking during his visit to the United States, President Irro said that strengthening internal peace and maintaining stable relations with neighboring administrations had been among his government’s priorities since taking office. He singled out Puntland as an important partner, saying the two sides had established practical cooperation in areas of security, counterterrorism and the fight against piracy. “When I came to office, one of my highest priorities was peace within Somaliland and peace with neighboring administrations. We established relations with Puntland and agreed to cooperate on peace, as well as on combating terrorism and piracy,” Irro said. Joint Committees Strengthen Dialogue According to President Irro, Somaliland and Puntland have established joint committees to maintain regular communication and address issues of mutual concern. The committees have reportedly held several meetings, including sessions in Nairobi and Addis Ababa, where officials discussed ways to strengthen cooperation and facilitate relations between communities on both sides. Among the understandings reached, Irro said, was an agreement to facilitate the movement of people and commercial shipments between the two sides. “Somaliland and Puntland established joint committees that meet regularly. The committees have met twice in Nairobi and Addis Ababa, and we agreed to facilitate the movement of people and shipments,” he said. Security and Economic Interests The cooperation described by Irro extends beyond political dialogue. Security appears to be one of its most important components, particularly in confronting terrorism, piracy and other cross-border security threats. For communities living and trading across the wider region, improved cooperation could also have practical economic benefits. Easier movement of people, vehicles and commercial goods can strengthen trade and reduce disruptions along important transportation routes. The emphasis on practical cooperation is particularly significant given the complex political history between Somaliland and Puntland. Rather than allowing sensitive political questions to prevent communication, the two sides appear to be creating mechanisms through which issues can be discussed directly. A More Mature Approach President Irro’s remarks suggest a pragmatic approach in which Somaliland and Puntland can cooperate where their interests overlap, even while more sensitive political questions remain unresolved. Regular communication between officials, security cooperation and efforts to facilitate trade and movement can help reduce misunderstandings and strengthen confidence between neighboring communities. If sustained, this approach could represent an important shift toward a more cordial, mature and interest-based relationship between Somaliland and Puntland—one focused less on political rhetoric and more on the practical needs of their people. For now, President Irro’s message is clear: despite differences that may remain, Somaliland and Puntland can build common ground through dialogue, security cooperation, trade and people-to-people relations.
