items.title: Madaxweynaha Somaliland  oo kulan la yeeshay gudiga Diwaangelinta ururada siyaasada
items.description: Madaxweynaha Somaliland oo kilan la yeeshay gudiga Diwaangelinta ururada siyaasada Madaxweynaha Jamhuuriyadda Somaliland, Mudane Cabdiraxmaan Maxamed Cabdillaahi (Cirro), ayaa maanta kulan muhiim ah la yeeshay Guddida Diiwaangelinta Ururrada Siyaasadda iyo Ansixinta Axsaabta Qaranka JSL (GDUS&AAQ), kaas oo diiradda lagu saaray xoojinta hannaanka dimuqraadiyadda, ku-dhaqanka iyo kor-joogtaynta shuruucda iyo gudashada waajibaadka Qaran ee ay Guddidu u xil-saaran tahay. Guddidan oo ah Hay’ad Qaran oo madax-bannaan ayaa waxa ay u xil-saaran tahay diiwaangelinta, kormeerka, kobcinta, iyo xallinta khilaafaadka Axsaabta Qaranka iyo Ururrada Siyaasadda. Guddida Diiwaangelinta Ururada Siyaasadda iyo Ansixinta Axsaabta Qaranka ayaa Madaxweynaha ugu xog waramay halka ay marayso shaqada guddidu, qorshaha mustaqbalka dhow iyo kan fog, iyo caqabadaha jira. Intii uu kulanku socday, xubnaha Guddida ayaa Madaxweynaha warbixin faah-faahsan ka siiyey hawlaha uga qabsoomay dhinacyada kala duwan ee nidaamka diimoqraadiyadda iyo axsaabta badan ee dalka, waxa ayna Madaxweynaha gudoonsiiyeen Qorshahooda Istraatejiyadda (Strategic Plan) ee sannadaha 2025 – 2026. Sidoo kale, Guddidu waxa ay Madaxweynaha la wadaagtay qorshaha dhow ee ah Casriyeynta hawl-qabadka Guddida oo ay ka mid tahay in dhammaan xogta ay kaydiso Guddidu laga dhigi doono mid electronic ah (Digital Data Base), qorshaha samaynta ‘Democracy Academy’, Qorshaha Dib-u-habaynta Diimoqraadiyadda, Dhiirigelinta ka-qayb-galka loo dhanyahay ee Diimoqraadiyadda, kobcinta Axsaabta Siyaasadda, iyo islaxisaabtanka iyo daahfurnaanta. Madaxweynaha Jamhuuriyadda Somaliland ayaa Guddida Diiwaangelinta Ururrada Siyaasadda iyo Ansixinta Axsaabta Qaranka ku bogaadiyey dedaalka iyo masuuliyadda ay Qaranka u hayaan, isaga oo ku boorriyey in ay dardargeliyaan oo ay dhammaystiraan hawlaha muhiimka ah ee horyaalla. Madaxweynaha Jamhuuriyadda Somaliland waxa uu Guddida u xaqiijiyey in Xukuumaddu ay garab taagan tahay Hay’addan Qaran ee u xilsaaran ilaalinta iyo horumarinta dimuqraadiyadda, isaga oo ku adkeeyey in ay si daacadnimo iyo xilkasnimo leh u gutaan waajibaadkooda, si loo sii xoojiyo dhaqanka dimuqraadiyadeed ee Somaliland iyo kalsoonida shacabka ee hay’adaha Qaranka.

items.title: Faah-faahinta markab maanta lagu afduubtay biyaha Soomaaliya
items.description: Muqdisho (Caasimada Online) – Markab xamuul ah ayaa lagu afduubtay meel ka baxsan xeebaha Soomaaliya, kadib markii koox hubeysan ay u suuragashay inay fuusho markabka oo ay la wareegto gacan-ku-hayntiisa. Hay’adda Hawl-gallada Ganacsiga Badda ee UK (UKMTO) ayaa sheegtay in dhacdadu ay dhacday Isniintii, iyadoo soo saartay digniin ku aaddan xaaladda amni ee markabka iyo nawaaxiga xeebaha Soomaaliya. Sida lagu sheegay warbixinta UKMTO, dhacdadu waxay ka dhacday qiyaastii afar mayl-badeed koonfur kaga beegan xeebaha Soomaaliya. Sarkaalka amniga ee shirkadda markabka ayaa hay’adda u sheegay in siddeed nin oo hubeysan oo aan fasax u haysan inay markabka fuulaan ay gudaha u galeen, kadibna ay gacanta ku dhigeen markabka. Ilaa hadda ma cadda cidda iska leh markabka la afduubtay iyo halka uu ku wajahnaa, iyadoo UKMTO aysan bixin faahfaahin dheeraad ah oo ku saabsan markabka ama kooxda qabsatay. Xeebaha Soomaaliya ayaa muddo dheer ahaa goob ay ka dhici jireen weerarro burcad-badeednimo, gaar ahaan intii u dhaxeysay 2008 iyo 2018, xilligaas oo maraakiib badan lagu afduubtay. Inkasta oo tallaabooyin amni iyo iskaashi caalami ah ay horseedeen hoos u dhac weyn oo ku yimid falalka burcad-badeednimada, haddana weerarro iyo afduubyo cusub ayaa dib uga soo muuqday xeebaha Soomaaliya dhammaadkii 2023. Dhacdadan cusub ayaa sare u qaadaysa walaaca laga qabo in burcad-badeednimadu ay mar kale ku soo xoogeysanayso xeebaha Soomaaliya, iyadoo hay’adaha amniga iyo kuwa maraakiibta ay si dhow ula socdaan xaaladda. Sarkaalka amniga ee shirkadda markabka ayaa hay’adda u sheegay in siddeed nin oo hubeysan oo aan fasax u haysan inay markabka fuulaan ay gudaha u galeen, kadibna ay gacanta ku dhigeen markabka. Ilaa hadda ma cadda cidda iska leh markabka la afduubtay iyo halka uu ku wajahnaa, iyadoo UKMTO aysan bixin faahfaahin dheeraad ah oo ku saabsan markabka ama kooxda qabsatay. Xeebaha Soomaaliya ayaa muddo dheer ahaa goob ay ka dhici jireen weerarro burcad-badeednimo, gaar ahaan intii u dhaxeysay 2008 iyo 2018, xilligaas oo maraakiib badan lagu afduubtay. Inkasta oo tallaabooyin amni iyo iskaashi caalami ah ay horseedeen hoos u dhac weyn oo ku yimid falalka burcad-badeednimada, haddana weerarro iyo afduubyo cusub ayaa dib uga soo muuqday xeebaha Soomaaliya dhammaadkii 2023. Dhacdadan cusub ayaa sare u qaadaysa walaaca laga qabo in burcad-badeednimadu ay mar kale ku soo xoogeysanayso xeebaha Soomaaliya, iyadoo hay’adaha amniga iyo kuwa maraakiibta ay si dhow ula socdaan xaaladda. items.title: EXCLUSIVE: Audit records and Documents reviewed by Daily Somalia raise serious questions over procurement, contracting and oversight at Somalia’s Civil Aviation Authority
items.description: MOGADISHU — Official audit records and supporting documents reviewed by Daily Somalia raise serious questions over procurement practices, private contracting and administrative controls within Somalia’s Civil Aviation Authority (SCAA), as the government continues to promote plans for rebuilding the country’s aviation sector. At the centre of the documents is a finding by the Office of the Auditor General that the Civil Aviation Authority entered into procurement agreements worth a combined $2,073,376.56 without registering them with the Auditor General’s office. The audit states that failure to register government contracts undermines transparency, accountability and the Auditor General’s ability to scrutinize public expenditure. The 2025 federal audit explains that the Auditor General is legally mandated to verify government contracts, monitor financial transactions and assess whether public institutions comply with Somalia’s financial-management and procurement laws. One company appearing in the aviation authority’s procurement records is One Complete Services Ltd, which is listed against a $12,532 contract. Documents reviewed by Daily Somalia show the company was registered on 10 October 2022. A commercial licence issued by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry identifies its business activity as “Facilities and Maintenance” and lists its address in Taleex, Hodan, Mogadishu. Daily Somalia has also received information alleging that the company, represented by Younis Mohamed Noor, became involved in additional services for the Civil Aviation Authority. The available audit record confirms the specific contract appearing in the document. It does not, on its own, establish the full value or extent of any wider business relationship between the company and SCAA. That distinction matters. What now requires scrutiny is whether additional contracts existed, how they were awarded, how much was paid, whether competitive procurement procedures were followed and whether any official connected to the Authority had a personal or financial interest in the arrangements. Questions for SCAA leadership The findings raise direct accountability questions for the management of the Civil Aviation Authority under Director General Ahmed Moallim Hassan. Somalia’s Auditor General states that directors-general and other senior officials of federal institutions are responsible for maintaining effective internal controls, managing financial risks and making sure government transactions comply with applicable laws. The central question is therefore not simply whether services were delivered. It is whether public contracts were awarded, registered, paid and supervised according to the law. Millions in airport revenue also questioned The latest federal audit identifies another major issue involving Somalia’s aviation sector. Under the concession agreement governing Aden Adde International Airport, the Federal Government is entitled to 25% of the gross revenue earned by Favori LLC, the private company operating the airport. According to the Auditor General, Favori reported approximately $29.71 million in revenue during 2025. That should have generated around $7.43 million for the Somali government. Government financial records, however, showed receipts of only about $4.15 million, leaving an audited difference of approximately $3.27 million. The Auditor General said the missing amount affected the completeness and accuracy of the government’s reported concession revenue. This finding concerns the government-Favori concession and should not be attributed to SCAA without further evidence. But it exposes another weakness in the financial controls surrounding one of Somalia’s most important public assets. Security questions at the airport Daily Somalia has separately received allegations involving the construction of an airport gate and an intervention by security authorities. Sources allege that the gate was constructed without the required prior coordination with relevant security agencies and was later closed following intervention by the National Intelligence and Security Agency, NISA. Further claims concern what happened following the closure, including an alleged dispute involving the private company representative and security services at the Authority. Daily Somalia has not independently verified these claims and is reporting them as allegations, not established facts. Given the security sensitivity of Aden Adde International Airport, the issue warrants an official investigation capable of determining who authorized the construction, which company performed the work, whether security approval existed and what actions followed NISA’s intervention. Allegations of exclusive access Daily Somalia has also received claims that foreign aviation companies operating in Somalia were directed to use services provided by a particular private company. No finding of wrongdoing can be made without examining the written instructions, contracts and relevant procurement records. If the allegation is substantiated, however, authorities would need to explain the legal basis for restricting companies to one provider and whether such an arrangement complied with procurement and competition rules. Ageing aviation systems There are also unresolved questions surrounding Somalia’s aviation infrastructure and the replacement of ageing technical systems. Information reviewed by Daily Somalia indicates that significant aviation equipment was inherited through earlier international aviation-management arrangements rather than purchased recently by the Federal Government. An accountable aviation authority should be able to publicly establish what safety-critical equipment is currently operating, when it was acquired, its expected operational lifespan, maintenance costs, replacement schedules and the procurement process for new systems. These are not minor administrative questions. They concern the systems responsible for managing aircraft moving through Somali airspace. What the evidence shows, and what it does not Daily Somalia’s review identifies two categories of information. Documented findings include: the Auditor General’s concerns over unregistered contracts, the listed $12,532 One Complete Services contract, and the approximately $3.27 million discrepancy in the government’s expected Favori concession revenue. The Auditor General’s broader 2025 review also examined compliance across 22 federal institutions, focusing specifically on procurement, personnel, assets and internal government controls. Other claims concerning additional contracts, the airport gate, security intervention and alleged exclusive service arrangements remain allegations requiring further evidence and official investigation. Daily Somalia will not present allegations as proven misconduct. But documented audit concerns cannot be dismissed simply because other parts of the case remain under investigation. The public deserves to know who received aviation contracts, how those contracts were awarded, what services were delivered, how much public money was paid, and who authorized the decisions. Questions have also emerged over the tenure and term limits of SCAA’s senior leadership, including Director General Ahmed Moallim Hassan. Greater clarity is needed on the legal duration of the Director General’s mandate, the date of his appointment, and whether any renewal or extension has been formally authorized. Publication of the relevant appointment decisions and legal provisions would help establish whether the current leadership remains within its prescribed mandate. Appointed acting head in 2018 and permanently confirmed on June 22, 2020, the Director General of the Somali Civil Aviation Authority has led the agency for eight years. Although Law No. 28 limits the term to four years renewable once, his mandate expired in June 2024. He remains in office despite changes in leadership and the expiration of his second term. This situation persists because Article 16(2) omits mandate expiration from the legal grounds for vacating office, attaching no consequences to a lapsed term. Without explicit provisions declaring the post vacant or requiring a succession process, enforcement relies entirely on executive discretion. Consequently, an aligned leadership can silently bypass term limits, leaving the regulator of sovereign airspace operating without a valid statutory mandate. items.title: Somalia president calls for AU peacekeepers to leave
items.description: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud declared on Sunday that Somalia no longer needs foreign peacekeepers to guarantee its own security, telling African Union troops it was time to go home even as the continental mission they serve in faces the most serious funding crisis of its two-decade history. “We have reached a point where we can now take full charge of our security. Let’s give African peacekeepers a bunch of flowers and send them home,” Mohamud said, speaking in Somalia’s central Galmudug state. The president made the remarks at a graduation ceremony marking the passing-out of roughly 3,000 newly trained Somali National Army soldiers – the largest single graduating class the country has produced since the collapse of its central government in 1991. The recruits, drawn from across Somalia, completed a full year of training in basic soldiering, military discipline and combat tactics. The graduation was delivered under a defence cooperation agreement Somalia signed with Saudi Arabia in February, through which Riyadh committed to training approximately 5,000 Somali soldiers; Sunday’s cohort accounts for the bulk of that pledge delivered in a single intake. Training took place at Hanan Bure in the Galgaduud region, a site Saudi military officials visited repeatedly over the course of the year to monitor progress. Instruction was delivered by foreign military personnel from Romania, Ukraine, Sudan and other countries — a composition some regional reporting has separately described as also drawing on trainers from South Africa and Colombia. Mohamud cast the graduation as proof of Somalia’s broader recovery, describing it as testament to the reconstruction of the country’s national army. A drawdown already under way The president’s call comes only days after Ethiopian troops serving under the African Union handed over their forward operating base in the southern Somali town of Burhakaba to Somali government forces, part of a phased drawdown already reshaping the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia, AUSSOM, and its predecessor missions. AUSSOM, which succeeded the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (ATMIS) on January 1, 2025, was itself designed around a gradual handover of security responsibility to Somali forces, continuing a process that began with the earlier AMISOM deployment in 2007. Somali authorities have said their forces assumed control of 23 former AU forward operating bases between January 2023 and April 2025. But the mission Mohamud is now urging out the door is also fighting for its own survival. AUSSOM’s current mandate expires on December 31, and the mission depends heavily on the UN Support Office in Somalia, UNSOS, for fuel, transport, medical care and other logistics. Washington has told the African Union it will not support renewing that UN logistical arrangement beyond the current mandate – while stopping short of blocking a renewal of AUSSOM’s mandate itself, provided an alternative source of logistical funding can be found. Somali officials are reported to be pressing Gulf states to help finance continued AU protection of key towns and infrastructure once the current arrangement lapses, though neither Mogadishu nor any Arab government has publicly confirmed such talks. A more crowded security picture, not a simpler one Mohamud’s invitation to African peacekeepers to leave does not mean Somalia is moving toward a purely national security posture. Turkey has built one of the most extensive bilateral military relationships in Mogadishu’s history, running training programmes through Camp TURKSOM since 2017 that have produced thousands of soldiers, including elite Gorgor commando units, and maintaining a troop presence its parliament has authorised to grow as large as 2,500. The United States continues to provide intelligence, training and air support. Egypt has joined the AU deployment itself, while Uganda and Ethiopia maintain forces in Somalia outside their formal AU commitments. The effect is a security architecture fragmenting from one dominant multinational African force into several parallel bilateral partnerships – with Saudi Arabia’s training programme now added to a list that already includes Turkey, the United States, Egypt, the UAE and others. A federal dispute in the background The president’s appearance in Galmudug carries political weight beyond the security announcement. His visit has sharpened tensions with neighbouring Puntland, which has placed its own security forces on alert and accused the federal government of stoking instability around Galkayo, a city split along the Puntland-Galmudug boundary. A stronger federal security presence in Galmudug would bolster Mogadishu’s hand in its wider standoff with more autonomous regional administrations, making Sunday’s graduation as much a marker in Somalia’s internal balance of power as in its relationship with foreign forces. items.title: Madaxweynaha Puntland oo la kulmay Saraakiisha Ciidamada ee Gobolka Mudug
items.description: Madaxweynaha Dowlad Goboleedka Puntland, Siciid Cabdullaahi Maxamed (Deni) oo booqasho ku jooga Magaalada Gaalkacyo ayaa caawa waqooyiga magaaladaasi kula kulmay Saraakiisha Ciidamada Puntland ee Gobolka Mudug. Madaxweynaha ayaa waxaa kulanka ku wehlinayay xubno ka mid ah Goleyaasha Dowlad Goboleedka Puntland iyo Taliyaha Ciidanka Daraawiishta Puntland, General Aadan Cabdi Xaashi, sida lagu sheegay qoraal la soo dhigay bogga wararka ee Madaxtooyada Puntland. Qoraalka laguma sheegin waxa uu Madaxweynuhu kala hadlay Saraakiisha Ciidamada Qalabka Sida ee ka hawlgala Gobolka Mudug, balse waxa uu kulankan imanaya, wax yar uun ka dib, markii Madaxweye Xasan Sheekh Maxamuud uu gaaray koonfurta Gaalkacyo oo Galmudug ay maamusho. Dowlad Goboleedka Puntland ayaa horey uga digtay safarka Madaxweynaha Dowladda Federaalka ee Gaalkacyo, iyadoo ku andacooneysa in uu uga gol leeyahay in uu colaad cusub kaga huriyo deegaanada Puntland, gaar ahaan Gaalkacyo. Saraakiisha Ciidamada Puntland ayaa Axaddii sheegay in la xiray xuduudaha Puntland, si looga hortago waxa ay ku sheegeen sharta Xasan Sheekh Maxamuud. Puntland ayaa ciidamo fara-badan ku soo daadisay waddooyinka xaafadaha ku yaala waqooyiga Gaalkacyo, taas oo keentay in Galmudug ay dhinaceeda gasho xaalad feejignaan ah. Dhaqdhaqaaqyada ciidan ee ka soo cusboonaaday labada qaybood ee Gaalkacyo ayaa xaddiday isu socodka shacabka ee magaalada.

items.title: Toddobo Tahriibe oo ku Dhintay Badda Liibiya iyo 50 Soomaali iyo Masaari ah oo la Badbaadiyay
items.description: TRIPOLI, Goobjoog — Toddobo qof ayaa ku dhintay safar tahriib oo ay kaga gudbayeen Badda Dhexe, halka 50 kale oo u dhashay Soomaaliya iyo Masar laga badbaadiyay doon alwaax ah oo ku jirtay biyaha caalamiga ah ee ka baxsan xeebaha Liibiya, sida ay maanta sheegtay hay’adda samafalka caafimaadka ee EMERGENCY. Markabka samatabbixinta Life Support, oo ay maamusho EMERGENCY, ayaa subaxnimadii Isniinta helay doonta oo ku jirtay aagga baadigoobka iyo samatabbixinta ee Liibiya. Toddoba qof ayaa dhintay intii safarku socday, halka laba ka mid ah dadka la badbaadiyey ay xaaladdoodu aad u liidato, iyagoo la ildaran neefqabatin una baahan in si degdeg ah loo daadgureeyo si ay daryeel caafimaad u helaan. Dadka badbaaday ayaa sheegay inay waaberigii 16ka Agoosto ka soo shiraacdeen magaalada xeebeedka Zuwara ee galbeedka Liibiya. EMERGENCY waxay sheegtay in dadka doonta saarnaa ay asal ahaan ka soo jeedaan Soomaaliya iyo Masar, inkasta oo aan weli si gaar ah loo shaacin tirada Soomaalida iyo Masaarida mid kasta. Kontonka qof ee la badbaadiyey waxay ka kooban yihiin 45 rag ah iyo shan dumar ah. Waxa si gaar ah walaac u leh in 29 ka mid ahi yihiin carruur aan cid weyn oo masuul ka ahi la socon; 26 waa wiilal, saddexna waa gabdho, sida ay EMERGENCY sheegtay. Hay’addu waxay masuuliyiinta ka codsatay in markabka loo qoondeeyo deked ammaan ah oo dhow, hasayeeshee markii danbe waxaa loo asteeyey Bari, oo ku taalla koonfurta Talyaaniga, si dadka la soo badbaadiyay halkaas looga dejiyo. Ilaa hadda lama shaacin da’da iyo jinsiyadaha toddobada qof ee geeriyooday, mana cadda inta ay Soomaalidu ka yihiin dadka dhintay ama kuwa xaaladdoodu halista tahay. Reuters waxay sheegtay in EMERGENCY aanay faahfaahin dheeraad ah ka bixin xaaladda labada qof ee u baahan daadguraynta caafimaad ee degdegga ah. Dhacdadan ayaa, mar kale, muujinaysa khatarta sii kordhaysa ee marinbiyoodka bartamaha Badda Dhexe, oo ah jidka ay tahriibayaal badan uga gudbaan Liibiya iyagoo iskudayaya inay gaaraan Yurub. Hay’adda Caalamiga ah ee Socdaalka ee IOM ayaa dhowaan sheegtay in 821 qof ay ku dhinteen ama ku lumeen marinbiyoodka Bartamaha Badda Dhexe (Mediterranean Sea) sannadkan 2026, xilli tirada dadka jidkan ku gaaraya Yurub ay hoos u dhacday. items.title: Markab Xamuul oo lagu Afduubtay Xeebaha Soomaaliya
items.description: MUQDISHO, Goobjoog — Markab xamuul ayaa galabnimadii maanta lagu afduubtay meel u dhow xeebaha Soomaaliya, kaddib markii siddeed nin oo hubaysan ay fuuleen markabka oo ay la wareegeen, sida ay sheegtay hay’adda UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO). Dhacdada ayaa la soo sheegay abbaaraha 11:36 UTC, oo ku beegan 2:36 galabnimo waqtiga Soomaaliya, waxayna ka dhacday qiyaastii afar mayl-badeed meel koonfur ka xigta degaanka Mareeyo ee xeebaha Soomaaliya. UKMTO ayaa sheegtay in xogta dhacdada ay ka heshay sarkaalka amniga ee shirkadda markabka. Nimanka hubaysan ayaa markii ay markabka fuuleen kaddib la wareegay gacan-ku-hayntiisa. Hay’adaha amniga badda ayaa baaraya dhacdada, halka xaaladda shaqaalaha markabka aan ilaa hadda si rasmi ah loo xaqiijin. UKMTO ma aysan shaacin magaca markabka, hasayeeshee shirkadda amniga badda ee Vanguard Tech ayaa sheegtay in markabka la afduubtay uu yahay Lutuf, oo ah markab xamuul oo ka diiwaangashan Cameroon. Xogta Equasis ee ay soo xigatay Seatrade Maritime News ayaa muujinaysa in markabka la sameeyay 1995, awooddiisa culaysqaadka guudna ay tahay 1,401 tan. Dhacdadan cusub ayaa timid xilli walaac isa soo taraya laga muujinayo dibusookordhidda falalka burcadbadeednimada ee xeebaha Soomaaliya. Xarunta Iskuduwidda Macluumaadka Badaha ee JMIC waxay 16kii Agoosto qiimaynteeda halista maraakiibta ku sheegtay mid dhexdhexaad ah, iyadoo tilmaantay inay weli jiraan weerarro fursadraac ah oo ka dhacaya xeebaha Soomaaliya. JMIC waxay sheegtay in ilaa 16kii Agoosto afar markab oo ganacsi ay gacanta ugu jireen kooxo burcadbadeed Soomaali ah: Honour 25, oo la afduubtay 21kii Abriil; Sward, oo la qabsaday 26kii Abriil; Eureka, oo la afduubtay 2dii Maajo; iyo Asana, oo gacanta lagu dhigay 17kii Luulyo. Haddii xogta markabka Lutuf si buuxda loo xaqiijiyo, wuxuu noqonayaa markabkii shanaad ee taxanahan cusub lagu daro. Ilaa hadda lama shaacin tirada iyo jinsiyadaha hawlwadeennada saaran Lutuf, nooca xamuulka uu sido, halka ay afduubayaashu ula dhaqaaqeen iyo haddii uu jiro dalab madaxfurasho ah.

items.title: Heavy Fighting Erupts in Baidoa as Rival Forces Battle for Control of Southwest Capital
items.description: Baidoa (WDN) — Heavy fighting has erupted inside Baidoa, transforming the capital of South West State into the latest and most dramatic flashpoint in Somalia’s deepening political and security crisis. The clashes are reportedly pitting forces loyal to former South West State President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Laftagareen” against forces aligned with the Federal Government of Somalia and supporting the administration led by Aden Mohamed Nur (Aden Madoobe). Fighting erupts, Baidoa, the interim capital of SW The intensity of the fighting has stunned residents, with reports of heavy gunfire and powerful explosions reverberating across different parts of the city. A spokesman for the Southwest administration aligned with Laftagareen claimed that his forces had captured parts of Baidoa, describing the operation as a “liberation struggle” and calling on residents to support the forces carrying out the offensive. A spokesman for Laftagareen’s forces also warned that troops deployed from Mogadishu would suffer defeat, referring to the expected confrontation as “Salbalaar.” The claims could not be independently verified. Meanwhile, residents reported sustained exchanges of heavy weapons and explosions in several areas of the city, underscoring the seriousness of the confrontation and the rapidly deteriorating security situation. Federal Government forces supporting the administration headed by Aden Madoobe are reportedly continuing to resist the assault. The battle has placed Baidoa at the center of an increasingly dangerous confrontation in which political disputes over leadership and legitimacy have spilled directly onto the streets. Neither the Federal Government nor the administration led by Aden Madoobe has issued a detailed official statement confirming the latest developments or providing verified information on casualties, territorial changes or the scale of the fighting. A City Caught in a Political Storm For now, Baidoa remains tense, with conflicting accounts emerging from the battlefield and independent verification proving difficult. The fighting represents more than another armed confrontation in Somalia. Baidoa is the political and administrative heart of South-west State, and any prolonged battle for control of the city could have consequences far beyond its streets. What is unfolding is therefore being watched with growing alarm: a political struggle that once played out through speeches, negotiations and competing claims of legitimacy has now erupted into open armed confrontation inside one of Somalia’s most important regional capitals. As gunfire continues to echo through Baidoa, the central question is no longer simply who controls the city—but whether Somalia’s political disputes can still be resolved through politics before the battlefield becomes the country’s principal negotiating table. Magaalada Gaalkacyo waxaa sidoo kale ku sugan Madaxweynaha Puntland Saciid Cabdullaahi Deni, kaas oo halkaasi ka wada kulamo uu la yeelanayo bulshada iyo dhinacyada siyaasadda, xilli uu sii xoogeysanayo khilaafka siyaasadeed ee u dhexeeya Puntland iyo Dowladda Federaalka. items.title: Somaliland Signals Diplomatic Restraint Over UN Visit to Las Anod
items.description: Hargeisa (WDN) — Somaliland has adopted a notably measured diplomatic posture following a visit to Las Anod by a United Nations delegation, acknowledging the mission while strongly implying that the visit was undertaken with the knowledge and approval of Somaliland authorities. In a statement issued in English, Somaliland’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it remained committed to facilitating humanitarian assistance, but emphasized that visits of this nature should be conducted through established diplomatic channels and in coordination with Somaliland. “We remain committed to facilitating humanitarian assistance. However, visits of this nature must follow established diplomatic protocols and be coordinated with the Somaliland authorities,” the ministry said. The carefully worded statement appears to serve two purposes. On the one hand, Somaliland sought to avoid confrontation with the United Nations and reaffirm its willingness to facilitate humanitarian operations. On the other, its reference to established diplomatic procedures appears designed to signal that Hargeisa was aware of—and, by implication, had given the necessary clearance for—the UN delegation’s visit to Las Anod. Although the statement does not explicitly say that Somaliland formally authorized the visit, its wording strongly suggests that Hargeisa considers itself an authority whose consent or coordination is required for international missions operating in the disputed area. Diplomatic Message Behind the Statement The distinction is politically significant. Las Anod is currently administered by the Northeast State, which is aligned with Somalia’s Federal Government and rejects Somaliland’s claim to sovereignty over Sool and surrounding territories. Somaliland, however, continues to regard the region as part of its territory. By stressing coordination with Somaliland authorities, Hargeisa appears to be reinforcing its longstanding diplomatic position without directly challenging the UN delegation or obstructing humanitarian engagement. The approach represents a relatively restrained response to an issue that could easily have triggered a sharper political confrontation. Rather than accusing the United Nations of violating its territorial claims, Somaliland has chosen to emphasize diplomatic protocol and humanitarian cooperation. This allows Hargeisa to assert its position while maintaining working relations with international organizations. Las Anod at the Center of Competing Claims The UN visit comes amid an increasingly complicated political and humanitarian environment in Las Anod. Since Somaliland forces withdrew from the city following intense fighting in 2023, Las Anod has emerged as the political center of the North Eastern State, which has subsequently strengthened its relationship with Mogadishu. The competing claims have turned the city into one of the most politically sensitive locations in the Horn of Africa. For international organizations, the situation creates a delicate balancing act. Humanitarian agencies must maintain access to communities in need while navigating competing claims of authority from Somaliland, the Federal Government of Somalia and the North Eastern State administration. Somaliland’s latest statement appears to recognize that reality while making clear that it expects international actors to maintain formal diplomatic engagement with Hargeisa. Northeast State Yet to Respond The Northeast State administration has not yet publicly responded to Somaliland’s statement or clarified its position regarding the UN delegation’s visit. The absence of an immediate response leaves an important question unanswered: Was the UN mission coordinated solely with the authorities in Las Anod, or did Somaliland’s authorities formally provide the clearance they now appear to suggest? For now, Somaliland’s diplomatic language is significant precisely because it stops short of making an explicit claim of authorization while nevertheless conveying that the mission was not entirely outside Hargeisa’s diplomatic framework. The episode once again demonstrates the extraordinary complexity surrounding Las Anod, where humanitarian access, territorial claims and competing political authorities increasingly intersect. For Somaliland, the message appears clear: humanitarian assistance should not be politicized, but international engagement in the disputed territory should also recognize Hargeisa’s claimed authority and diplomatic standing. items.title: Shock and despair in Mogadishu as Hundreds of Poor Families Face Eviction in Waaberi
items.description: Mogadishu (WDN) — Shock and despair are spreading through the Buulo Eelaay neighborhood of Waaberi district, where hundreds of mostly low-income families say they have been ordered to leave homes they have occupied for decades, amid fears that bulldozers could soon arrive to demolish the properties. Residents say they were given only a few days to vacate their homes. Many families have already begun moving their belongings, using small vehicles and donkey carts to transport what they can salvage. For families living on the margins, the order has created an immediate humanitarian crisis. Women, children and elderly residents are among those being forced to confront an agonizing question: Where will we go? Some families say they have neither the money to rent alternative accommodation nor the resources to cover the cost of moving. Others say they have received no clear information about whether the government has prepared relocation sites, compensation or any form of assistance. “We do not know where we are supposed to go,” residents told WDN, describing a growing sense of fear and uncertainty across the neighborhood. Buulo Eelaay, part of the Hantiwadaag area of Waaberi, is one of Mogadishu’s older neighborhoods. Its densely packed homes and narrow streets reflect decades of urban growth, with many residents saying their families have lived there for generations. Residents argue that successive governments, including previous civilian administrations and the former military government, refrained from forcibly removing long-established families because of the economic vulnerability of the communities and the particular circumstances surrounding the area. The latest developments have nevertheless reopened a much larger and increasingly bitter debate over land ownership in Mogadishu. Buulo Eelaay is reportedly not the only part of Mogadishu where residents have faced eviction or demolition in recent weeks. Similar complaints have emerged from parts of Tokyo neighborhood in Yaqshiid district, Karaan district and areas behind Juba Hotel. Opposition politicians have also accused the Federal Government of pursuing a broader campaign to reclaim or reorganize land occupied by civilians, warning that the approach could trigger a new wave of displacement among some of the capital’s poorest residents. Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed, now a prominent opposition figure, has sharply criticized the government’s handling of land disputes, accusing the administration of what he described as the “auctioning” and seizure of public and privately occupied land. “This is a major disaster that we condemn,” Sharif said, arguing that the government had moved from public land to settlements established during the collapse of the state and was now targeting properties that citizens claim to legally own. Development or Displacement? For families in Buulo Eelaay, the distinction is becoming increasingly difficult to see. Urban redevelopment may require roads to be widened, land to be reorganized and informal settlements to be regularized. But where families have lived for decades, any intervention raises difficult questions about property rights, due process, consultation and compensation. Without clear answers, the bulldozer becomes more than a construction machine. It becomes a symbol of state power confronting people with little political or economic influence. Residents are therefore calling on the government to suspend the eviction process, consult affected communities and establish a transparent mechanism for determining ownership and resolving disputes. They also want authorities to clarify what will happen to families who are removed: Will they receive alternative housing? Compensation? Relocation assistance? Or simply be left to fend for themselves? So far, residents say they have received few convincing answers. The controversy comes at a particularly sensitive moment for Somalia, when political tensions are already high and public confidence in state institutions remains fragile. For a government seeking to strengthen its legitimacy, the treatment of vulnerable citizens during urban redevelopment could prove politically consequential. Mogadishu needs roads, modern infrastructure and orderly land administration. But it also needs something equally fundamental: a government that protects its citizens while developing their city. For the families of Buulo Eelaay, that principle is no longer an abstract question of governance. It is a question of whether they will still have a home when the bulldozers arrive. items.title: Madaxweyne Xasan Sheekh oo gaaray Magaalada Gaalkacyo (SAWIRRO)
items.description: Madaxweynaha Jamhuuriyadda Somaliya, Xasan Sheekh Maxamuud oo uu wehliyo Madaxweynaha Dowlad Goboleedka Galmudug, Axmed Cabdi Kaariye (Qoorqoor) ayaa gelinkii dambe ee maanta gaaray Magaalada Gaalkacyo ee Xarunta Gobolka Mudug. Madaxda ayaa si diiran loogu soo dhaweeyay Garoonka Kubadda Cagta Cabdullaahi Ciise, halkaas oo ay kula hadleen dad fara-badan oo kuwa deegaanka ah. Madaxweyne Xasan Sheekh ayaa dadka reer Gaalkacyo uga mahadceliyay soo dhaweynta ballaaran ee ay ugu sameeyeen magaalada, isagoona ku amaanay, sida ay u ilaalinayaan midnimada iyo wadajirka dhexdooda. Madaxweynaha Dowladda Federaalka ayaa muddada uu ku sugan yahay magaalada kulamo kula qaadan doona bulshada qaybaheeda kala duwan. Magaalada ayaa waxaa la geeyay boqolaal ka tirsan Ciidanka Xoogga Dalka, si ay kuwa Galmudug uga gacan siiyaan sugidda amniga ee wafdiga Madaxweynaha. Madaxweyne Xasan Sheekh ayaa gaaray Gaalkacyo, iyadoo Puntland ay digniin ka soo saartay imaanshiiisa magaalada, ka dib markii ay ku eedeysay in uu colaad cusub ka hurinayo gudaha Puntland. Galmudug ayaa Puntland ku gacan seyrtay in laga hortago safarka Madaxweynaha ee Gaalkacyo, iyadoona Galmudug ay sheegtay in Madaxweynuhu uu xaq u leeyahay in xilli kasta uu soo booqdo deegaanada Galmudug. Xaaladda Gaalkacyo ayaa ah mid xasaasi ah, iyadoo Puntland ay ku dhawaaqday in la hakiyay dhaqdhaqaaqyadii siyaasadeed ee magaalada, muddada uu Madaxweyne Xasan Sheekh ku sugan yahay magaaladaasi. Puntland ayaan ogoleyn in la tago koonfurta Gaalkacyo iyo in dad halkaasi ka socda ay soo galaan dhinaca waqooyi ee magaalada. Go’aankan ayaad mooddaa in si gaar ah loogu beegsanayo Odayaasha Dhaqanka ee reer Puntland ee la rabo inay koonfurta Gaalkacyo kula kulmaan Madaxweyne Xasan Sheekh.

items.title: Booliska Bari iyo INTERPOL oo Ka Wada Hadlay Iskaashiga Amniga+SAWIRO
items.description: Boosaaso (Raxanreeb Online): Taliyaha Qaybta Booliska Gobolka Bari, G/Sare Saciid Aadan Saciid, ayaa xafiiskiisa ku qaabilay guddi ka socday INTERPOL, iyadoo kulanka looga hadlay xoojinta iskaashiga iyo wada-shaqeynta dhinacyada amniga. Kulanka ayaa si gaar ah diiradda loogu saaray is-dhaafsiga xogaha amni, ka hortagga dambiyada abaabulan, iyo sidii loo sii xoojin lahaa wada-shaqeynta hay’adaha amniga Gobolka Bari iyo INTERPOL. Taliyaha ayaa adkeeyay muhiimadda ay leedahay wada-shaqeyn joogto ah oo dhex marta hay’adaha amniga gudaha iyo kuwa caalamiga ah, si loo xoojiyo amniga, loo yareeyo dambiyada, loona xaqiijiyo kala dambeyn waarta. Ugu dambeyn, Taliyaha ayaa guddiga INTERPOL uga mahadceliyay booqashadooda iyo dadaallada ay ku bixinayaan xoojinta iskaashiga dhinacyada amniga. items.title: Born From Collapse: The Real Story of How Somali Piracy Began
items.description: Somali piracy is often introduced as a story about criminals attacking ships from speedboats. That description captures the violence, but not the history. The phenomenon grew from state collapse, economic desperation, foreign exploitation of marine resources, weak maritime enforcement, and the opportunities created by a major shipping corridor that hosts roughly 20,000 vessels annually, carrying 12% of global seaborne trade. It was neither a simple popular uprising nor an inevitable product of Somali culture: it was a changing political economy that developed on land and at sea. Before the Pirate Boom Understanding Somali piracy requires distinguishing piracy from armed robbery, illegal fishing, maritime terrorism, and fishing-community conflicts under international law. While the Horn of Africa had a long maritime history, piracy was relatively uncommon before the modern Somali state was established. Coastal conflicts did exist, but they were not part of a continuous pirate tradition. The decisive break came with the collapse of the Somali state in 1991. This collapse created a profound institutional vacuum: when a state loses the capacity to police territory, enforce contracts, and punish violence, authority does not disappear, it fragments. In this vacuum, local elders, militias, businessmen, smugglers, and armed entrepreneurs began to compete over who can provide protection and collect revenue. The first recorded incidents of modern piracy occurred almost immediately after the collapse, specifically between 1991 and 1994 along the northeastern coast of Puntland and the central Mudug region. Early reports confirmed that in the absence of a navy, foreign trawlers began harvesting an estimated $300 million worth of seafood illegally each year. Somalia’s coastline became vulnerable not simply because the country was poor, but because no reliable institution could decide who had the right to fish, patrol, license vessels, or settle disputes. This vulnerability is best explained by political ecology, which connects environmental resources to power: fish stocks, coastal waters, and shipping lanes were not merely natural features, they were sources of wealth whose control changed after 1991. When foreign fishing fleets entered poorly regulated waters and local communities lost access to familiar livelihoods, environmental pressure became a political grievance. The end of centralized authority weakened policing, courts, coastguard functions, licensing systems, and the ability to regulate foreign access to Somali waters. Coastal communities were left with few legal economic opportunities while foreign vessels could operate with limited oversight. The early emergence and local tolerance of piracy are deeply connected to statelessness, poverty, illegal fishing, and toxic-waste dumping. Political ecology does not excuse piracy, rather, it explains how resource depletion and unequal control can create the resentment and insecurity in which armed markets grow. UNEP reports from 2005 documented the washing up of rusted containers following the 2004 Tsunami, providing physical evidence of the toxic waste dumping that occurred during the 1990s.  This history describes piracy’s origins as a political-ecological sequence in which governance collapse and resource exploitation disrupted coastal livelihoods and increased maritime insecurity. This does not mean that every pirate began as a fisherman defending Somali waters. The collapse of governance changed incentives for several groups at once, some saw armed protection or attacks on foreign vessels as income, while others entered a profitable criminal market once ransom became available. Claims of defending Somali waters and the commercial reality of hostage-taking could coexist. From Protection to Organized Crime Somali piracy developed as a cycle with distinct politically connected phases, tracing its path from the early 1990s through the dramatic rise after 2006. This framework rejects the idea that piracy appeared suddenly in 2008. While the international community noticed the crisis most clearly after attacks on World Food Programme vessels, the underlying conditions had been developing for years. This evolution is supported by the opportunity theory of crime: organized crime requires a suitable target, weak protection, expected profits, and a reasonable chance of escape. Somalia’s location beside one of the world’s busiest shipping routes supplied those conditions, offering targets ranging from small dhows to Ultra Large Crude Carriers. The transformation accelerated when hijacking ships for ransom became more profitable than opportunistic theft. Ransom transformed scattered maritime violence into a business, the target was valuable, the crew could be used as leverage, and the operation could be financed through networks onshore. World Bank data suggests that between 2005 and 2012, an estimated $339 million to $413 million was paid in total ransoms. As the business model matured, specific coastal towns evolved into specialized piracy hubs. Logistical nerve centers such as Eyl and Garacad in the north, alongside Hobyo and Harardhere in central Somalia, became the primary locations where hijacked vessels were anchored and negotiations were conducted. Between 2005 and 2011, attacks surged, peaking in 2011 with 176 reported attacks and 25 successful hijackings in a single year. Somali pirates became known for holding crews and cargoes hostage while negotiating their release. The operation required boats, weapons, fuel, intelligence, financiers, negotiators, safe houses, and intermediaries. Finally, the idea of social legitimacy helps explain why some coastal communities in these hubs tolerated pirates. A group can be criminal in international law while presenting itself locally as a protector, employer, or defender against foreign exploitation. That claim may be selective or fraudulent, but it can still create cooperation, silence, or access to supplies. Somali piracy therefore combined coercion with persuasion, its strength came not only from guns and boats, but also from the ability of pirate groups to embed themselves in local economies. In some hubs, the piracy economy was so integrated that local shops provided credit to pirate crews, to be repaid doubled (Dheef-Koror) only after a successful ransom was collected. Piracy economies are dynamic, actors, tactics, and incentives change, and a wide network of participants joined as the activities expanded following the collapse of the formal economy. Illegal fishing, piracy, counter-piracy, fraudulent negotiators, and foreign and local intermediaries all became deeply entangled. Why the Coast Mattered The relationship between piracy and fishing was never simple. Somali communities had legitimate grievances about foreign fishing and the loss of control over marine resources. Yet local actors also committed predation, competed over fishing rents, and sometimes cooperated with smugglers, officials, or pirate networks. Naval presence eventually contributed to a decline in piracy, but coastal engagement was deeper than many accounts assume. The maritime predatory trap cannot be broken without treating former pirate communities as partners in a legitimate blue economy. Regional evidence shows that illegal and foreign fishing, weak governance, restricted access to fishing grounds, and criminal activity were major drivers. Conflict was particularly concentrated in Kenyan and Somali waters and the southern Red Sea, meaning piracy belonged to a larger maritime-governance crisis that cost the global economy an estimated $7 billion to $12 billion annually at its height. Why Piracy Declined The dramatic decline in attacks after 2011 resulted from a combination of international naval patrols, improved coordination, ship protection, and, crucially, a shift in local political and social conditions. While effective naval measures reduced piracy in the Gulf of Aden, they often displaced activity further into the Indian Ocean. By 2012, over 30 nations had deployed more than 40 warships to the region, creating the most intensive naval cooperation since World War II. A decisive factor in this shift was the emergence of local Somali security actors, most notably the Puntland Maritime Police Force (PMPF). Established in 2010 with support from the United Arab Emirates, the PMPF became the only local force capable of conducting sustained counter-piracy operations on land. With a force that eventually grew to over 500 trained personnel, the PMPF targeted pirate logistics and blocked access to traditional anchorages in hubs like Eyl and Garacad. The presence of the PMPF allowed the Puntland government to assert control over the coastline, preventing criminal networks from returning to the same bays to dock hijacked vessels. Equally important was a community-led social movement driven by traditional Somali leaders. Under the administration of Puntland President Abdirahman Farole, a community-centered approach was adopted to strip piracy of its social legitimacy. Religious sheikhs were mobilized to issue fatwas declaring piracy as forbidden (haram), while clan elders were encouraged to dissuade young men from joining pirate gangs. In Eyl and Garacad, once the world’s most notorious pirate capital, the local community eventually turned on the pirates, physically chasing them out of the town in 2011. However, the decline should not be confused with the resolution of piracy’s root causes. Counter-piracy measures addressed only the symptoms of the crisis, such as maritime insecurity and weak law enforcement, while leaving triggers like corruption and economic dislocation intact. Traditional income-sharing arrangements helped contain conflict in some regions, but Puntland remained more vulnerable due to its proximity to deep-water shipping lanes and the survival of underground criminal infrastructures. This regional evidence suggests that while the PMPF and community leaders successfully suppressed the era of high-seas piracy, they did so within a fragile land-sea political economy that remained susceptible to future collapse. The Unfinished Story The most recent sources argue that Somali piracy is dormant rather than extinguished. A 2026 perspective links renewed risk to unresolved governance failures, illegal fishing, environmental degradation, and the survival of criminal networks. The resurgence began showing early signs with the hijacking of the MV Ruen in late 2023, the first successful capture of a merchant vessel in over six years. A major catalyst for this renewed activity was the shifting security landscape on land, specifically the withdrawal of the Puntland Maritime Police Force (PMPF) from the strategic Mudug and Garacad shoreline to address insurgency in the Bari and Sanag mountains. This reallocation removed a primary arm of deterrence that had historically played a massive role in securing the Mudug coast. Furthermore, systemic unemployment among the coastal youth has reached critical levels. Despite the completion of the Garacad Port, the facility has yet to generate sustainable employment for local youth, leaving many with no viable economic future. This lack of opportunity is exacerbated by a severe economic crisis caused by the sharp cutting of international humanitarian funding in 2025 and 2026. Amidst this hardship, the successful hijacking of the MV Abdullah in April 2024, which yielded a $5 million ransom, has served as a powerful motivational trigger. For youth seeing their comrades make massive amounts of money in a matter of weeks, it has encouraged a new generation to venture far beyond Somali territorial waters. This resurgence after 2022 exposes the limits of deterrence when community grievances and pirate networks remain intact. Onshore governance gaps and criminal infrastructure remain blind spots in counter-piracy policy. The real story of Somali piracy begins with the collapse of institutions governing Somalia’s coast. It grew when resource insecurity met criminal opportunity, became organized through political and commercial networks centered in hubs like Garacad and Eyl, and declined when international force raised the cost of attacks. State collapse created the institutional space, resource conflict supplied grievances, shipping created opportunity, and local legitimacy helped convert individual attacks into a durable political economy. Its possible return shows that naval deterrence can suppress piracy without repairing the land-sea political economy that produced it. A lasting solution must protect shipping while restoring coastal livelihoods, regulating fisheries, strengthening legitimate authority, and addressing the networks that profit from insecurity. items.fullContent: Somali piracy is often introduced as a story about criminals attacking ships from speedboats. That description captures the violence, but not the history. The phenomenon grew from state collapse, economic desperation, foreign exploitation of marine resources, weak maritime enforcement, and the opportunities created by a major shipping corridor that hosts roughly 20,000 vessels annually, carrying 12% of global seaborne trade. It was neither a simple popular uprising nor an inevitable product of Somali culture: it was a changing political economy that developed on land and at sea. Before the Pirate Boom Understanding Somali piracy requires distinguishing piracy from armed robbery, illegal fishing, maritime terrorism, and fishing-community conflicts under international law. While the Horn of Africa had a long maritime history, piracy was relatively uncommon before the modern Somali state was established. Coastal conflicts did exist, but they were not part of a continuous pirate tradition. The decisive break came with the collapse of the Somali state in 1991. This collapse created a profound institutional vacuum: when a state loses the capacity to police territory, enforce contracts, and punish violence, authority does not disappear, it fragments. In this vacuum, local elders, militias, businessmen, smugglers, and armed entrepreneurs began to compete over who can provide protection and collect revenue. The first recorded incidents of modern piracy occurred almost immediately after the collapse, specifically between 1991 and 1994 along the northeastern coast of Puntland and the central Mudug region. Early reports confirmed that in the absence of a navy, foreign trawlers began harvesting an estimated $300 million worth of seafood illegally each year. Somalia’s coastline became vulnerable not simply because the country was poor, but because no reliable institution could decide who had the right to fish, patrol, license vessels, or settle disputes. This vulnerability is best explained by political ecology, which connects environmental resources to power: fish stocks, coastal waters, and shipping lanes were not merely natural features, they were sources of wealth whose control changed after 1991. When foreign fishing fleets entered poorly regulated waters and local communities lost access to familiar livelihoods, environmental pressure became a political grievance. The end of centralized authority weakened policing, courts, coastguard functions, licensing systems, and the ability to regulate foreign access to Somali waters. Coastal communities were left with few legal economic opportunities while foreign vessels could operate with limited oversight. The early emergence and local tolerance of piracy are deeply connected to statelessness, poverty, illegal fishing, and toxic-waste dumping. Political ecology does not excuse piracy, rather, it explains how resource depletion and unequal control can create the resentment and insecurity in which armed markets grow. UNEP reports from 2005 documented the washing up of rusted containers following the 2004 Tsunami, providing physical evidence of the toxic waste dumping that occurred during the 1990s.  This history describes piracy’s origins as a political-ecological sequence in which governance collapse and resource exploitation disrupted coastal livelihoods and increased maritime insecurity. This does not mean that every pirate began as a fisherman defending Somali waters. The collapse of governance changed incentives for several groups at once, some saw armed protection or attacks on foreign vessels as income, while others entered a profitable criminal market once ransom became available. Claims of defending Somali waters and the commercial reality of hostage-taking could coexist. From Protection to Organized Crime Somali piracy developed as a cycle with distinct politically connected phases, tracing its path from the early 1990s through the dramatic rise after 2006. This framework rejects the idea that piracy appeared suddenly in 2008. While the international community noticed the crisis most clearly after attacks on World Food Programme vessels, the underlying conditions had been developing for years. This evolution is supported by the opportunity theory of crime: organized crime requires a suitable target, weak protection, expected profits, and a reasonable chance of escape. Somalia’s location beside one of the world’s busiest shipping routes supplied those conditions, offering targets ranging from small dhows to Ultra Large Crude Carriers. The transformation accelerated when hijacking ships for ransom became more profitable than opportunistic theft. Ransom transformed scattered maritime violence into a business, the target was valuable, the crew could be used as leverage, and the operation could be financed through networks onshore. World Bank data suggests that between 2005 and 2012, an estimated $339 million to $413 million was paid in total ransoms. As the business model matured, specific coastal towns evolved into specialized piracy hubs. Logistical nerve centers such as Eyl and Garacad in the north, alongside Hobyo and Harardhere in central Somalia, became the primary locations where hijacked vessels were anchored and negotiations were conducted. Between 2005 and 2011, attacks surged, peaking in 2011 with 176 reported attacks and 25 successful hijackings in a single year. Somali pirates became known for holding crews and cargoes hostage while negotiating their release. The operation required boats, weapons, fuel, intelligence, financiers, negotiators, safe houses, and intermediaries. Finally, the idea of social legitimacy helps explain why some coastal communities in these hubs tolerated pirates. A group can be criminal in international law while presenting itself locally as a protector, employer, or defender against foreign exploitation. That claim may be selective or fraudulent, but it can still create cooperation, silence, or access to supplies. Somali piracy therefore combined coercion with persuasion, its strength came not only from guns and boats, but also from the ability of pirate groups to embed themselves in local economies. In some hubs, the piracy economy was so integrated that local shops provided credit to pirate crews, to be repaid doubled (Dheef-Koror) only after a successful ransom was collected. Piracy economies are dynamic, actors, tactics, and incentives change, and a wide network of participants joined as the activities expanded following the collapse of the formal economy. Illegal fishing, piracy, counter-piracy, fraudulent negotiators, and foreign and local intermediaries all became deeply entangled. Why the Coast Mattered The relationship between piracy and fishing was never simple. Somali communities had legitimate grievances about foreign fishing and the loss of control over marine resources. Yet local actors also committed predation, competed over fishing rents, and sometimes cooperated with smugglers, officials, or pirate networks. Naval presence eventually contributed to a decline in piracy, but coastal engagement was deeper than many accounts assume. The maritime predatory trap cannot be broken without treating former pirate communities as partners in a legitimate blue economy. Regional evidence shows that illegal and foreign fishing, weak governance, restricted access to fishing grounds, and criminal activity were major drivers. Conflict was particularly concentrated in Kenyan and Somali waters and the southern Red Sea, meaning piracy belonged to a larger maritime-governance crisis that cost the global economy an estimated $7 billion to $12 billion annually at its height. Why Piracy Declined The dramatic decline in attacks after 2011 resulted from a combination of international naval patrols, improved coordination, ship protection, and, crucially, a shift in local political and social conditions. items.title: AUSSOM Cannot Eradicate Al-Shabaab Without Somali Government’s Full Engagement in the Fight
items.description: By Djama Mahamoud Ali The fight against Al-Shabaab has defined Somalia’s security landscape for nearly two decades. The Al-Qaeda affiliate has proven remarkably resilient against numerous counterinsurgency campaigns, exploiting the Somali government’s lack of appetite to fight against Alshabab, clan divisions, and persistent political crises. The international community has responded with substantial commitments, the African Union has maintained a peacekeeping presence since 2007, transitioning from AMISOM to ATMIS and most recently to AUSSOM, whose mandate extends through December 2026. The United States conducts airstrikes in coordination with the federal government and has completed the creation and training of the Somali Danab elite unit for counterterrorism operations. Turkey has built a parallel security architecture including the TURKSOM Military Training Academy, which has trained thousands of Somali soldiers, including members of the elite Gorgor Commando Brigade. Yet the results have been disappointing. By 2025, Al-Shabaab had launched a broad offensive, taking control of dozens of towns and villages. In August 2026 alone, the extremist group seized the strategic town of Teedaan in central Somalia’s Hiiraan region following intense fighting with government forces. The much-touted “Total War” against Al-Shabaab, launched in 2022, relied on fragile clan-militia alliances and was quickly derailed by political rifts This failure is not primarily military but political. The Somali federal government, under President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, has systematically deployed internationally trained and equipped forces not against Al-Shabaab but against its own federal member states and political opponents. Unless Somalia’s internal political divisions are resolved, the fight against Al-Shabaab cannot succeed. Jubaland Confrontation The federal government’s campaign against Jubaland represents the most significant and costly misdirection of military assets. In December 2024, armed clashes broke out between Somali federal forces and troops loyal to the Jubaland administration in Raskamboni, a strategic town in the Lower Jubba region near the Kenyan border. The federal government had deployed troops to Raskamboni after disagreeing with the outcome of Jubaland polls in which Ahmed Islam Mohamed Madobe was re-elected as president. The operation ended in catastrophic defeat of Somalia’s federal forces. Jubaland forces managed to neutralize the elite Gorgor troops, forcing some to seek refuge in Kenya. Senior Jubaland officials confirmed that 240 federal soldiers surrendered to Jubaland forces, further consolidating their control in the area. The federal troops suffered heavy defeats and were forced to retreat across the Kenyan border. This conflict displaced over 24,000 individuals. The Raskamboni debacle was not an isolated incident. In July 2025, clashes between federal troops and Jubaland forces near Beled-Hawo killed at least 10 people. The SNA forces suffered a major defeat in the December 2024 battle at Raskamboni,  As one analysis observed, the federal government “has entirely failed to learn the lessons of Ras Kamboni”. Federal lawmakers from Jubaland accused the federal government of deliberately preparing and financing militias to create insecurity along the border and disrupt peace. The pattern is unmistakable, internationally trained and equipped forces intended for counterterrorism were instead deployed against a federal member state and were defeated. South-West State Confrontation The most brazen example of military diversion occurred in March 2026, when federal troops forcibly removed Southwest State President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen. Laftagareen, in power since 2018, was re-elected with 66 percent of the vote but the federal government rejected the result as a “ploy” to hold onto power. Since the previous week, federal troops including Turkish-trained special units of the Somali military had been advancing on Baidoa, 246 kilometers southwest of Mogadishu, with instructions to oust Abdiaziz.This military operation used Turkish-trained Gorgor special forces and Turkish-supplied drones. Southwest State authorities accused Turkey of involvement in the military operations, alleging that Turkish-trained forces, equipment, and drones were used in actions against the administration. Laftagareen was forced to resign on March 30, 2026, and was allowed to fly into exile in Nairobi. The African Union called for restraint, warning that rising tensions between the federal government and Southwest State risked undermining the country’s stability. Renewed fighting continued in Baidoa through July 2026, with forces loyal to Laftagareen taking control of parts of the town while the national army mobilized troops to drive them away. Political Opponents Confrontation Beyond conflicts with member states, the federal government used military forces against domestic political opponents within the capital itself. On June 4, 2026, heavy fighting rocked Mogadishu as government forces and militias aligned with opposition leaders exchanged gunfire. The clashes erupted ahead of planned anti-government demonstrations challenging President Mohamud’s leadership and recent constitutional changes. Former Somalia President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed accused government forces of surrounding and attacking his residence, while former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire alleged that security forces used heavy weapons in densely populated areas and targeted senior opposition figures. Former National Intelligence and Security Agency Director Sanbaloolshe accused President Mohamud of targeting him, Khaire, and traditional elders during the fighting. The violence had devastating humanitarian consequences. Armed clashes between federal government forces and an opposition-affiliated armed group killed at least 13 people, injured 189 others, and displaced about 12,500 households. The fighting began near Dabka junction before spreading into densely populated areas including Hawlwadaag, Abdiaziz, Hodan, Wardhigley, and parts of Karaan. The United States and the United Kingdom condemned the violence, with the U.S. Embassy describing the clashes as reckless. As one opposition politician stated, “forces trained and equipped by international partners were used against political gatherings instead of being deployed strictly for counterterrorism operations.” Puntland Confrontation The most dramatic illustration of the federal government’s misdirection of military assets occurred on August 5, 2026. Heavily armed Puntland forces, backed by military vehicles, launched an operation against a Federal military camp near Galkayo airport. The Army was brought there to conduct operation against Puntland. Howevere, Puntland forces took full control of the camp and detained 101 militia members aligned with the federal government, including senior commanders. They also seized weapons, military vehicles, police uniforms, and other security equipment, including items claimed to be part of Chinese aid provided to the Somali Police Force. Puntland President Said Abdullahi Deni accused the federal government of fueling tensions by deploying troops and weapons to the area. “The operation carried out by Puntland forces in Galkayo sends a clear message to anyone engaged in activities that threaten Puntland’s security and state authority,” Deni said. He warned that any consequences would be the federal government’s responsibility and urged Hassan Sheikh to “change course before the crisis deepens”. Jubaland backed Puntland’s actions, stating that “weapons and military equipment were being moved into peaceful areas while Somali forces fighting Al-Shabaab were facing shortages of arms and supplies”. This statement underscores a devastating irony: international military aid intended for the counterterrorism fight is being diverted to internal political conflicts, while frontline forces against Al-Shabaab lack adequate resources. The confrontation was triggered by a disputed shipment of weapons allegedly transported by the federal government into southern Galkayo. Puntland President Deni accused the federal government of backing rival forces and attempting to interfere in Puntland’s internal affairs. Internal Political disagreement and Constitutional Crisis were the bases At the heart of these conflicts lies a broader constitutional crisis. In March 2026, parliament unilaterally approved a package of constitutional amendments hailed by government supporters as the culmination of a fourteen-year constitutional review process. However, opposition leaders and federal member states argue the changes could extend President Mohamud’s tenure and delay national elections. Relations between Mogadishu and several federal member states remain strained. Multiple state and deputy ministers representing Puntland, Jubaland, and Southwest have stepped down as tensions escalated over constitutional revisions and the framework for upcoming federal and regional elections.  The heart of Somalia’s recurrent election crisis is tension between the clan-based power-sharing system and direct elections, a conflict made harder to resolve because the distribution of power between the federal government and its member states is not clearly demarcated in the provisional constitution. The federal government’s unilateral constitutional amendments, enforced through military means using Turkish-trained forces, have alienated member states and deepened the political crisis. Al-Shabaab Exploits Internal Divisions  The diversion of military resources toward internal political objectives has direct and measurable consequences for the counterterrorism effort. Political tensions in Somalia have fueled concerns over security and stability, with analysts warning that political divisions could undermine recent security gains and complicate efforts to combat Al-Shabaab. Observers warn that if political divisions persist, they could erode international confidence in Somalia’s stabilization efforts and affect continued support from development and security partners. A letter from opposition leaders to the international community accused Somalia’s government of failing to “sustain progress against al-Shabaab, take ownership of its security functions, or undertake serious security sector reform,” blaming “internal rivalries and political infighting”. Al-Shabaab has been quick to exploit these divisions. The group launched a broad offensive in 2025, taking control of dozens of towns and villages. In August 2026, Al-Shabaab seized the strategic town of Teedaan in central Somalia following heavy fighting with government forces and allied local militias. The group’s current advance, which it calls Operation Ramadan, began in February 2025. Meanwhile, Somalia’s political class remains “dangerously polarized and unable to forge a united front against their common enemy, al Shabaab.” The juxtaposition is damning: while Al-Shabaab closes in on Mogadishu, the federal government uses its military to fight Puntland, oust regional presidents, and suppress political opposition. It is clear that political fragmentation hinders the fight against Al-Shabaab. If political divisions continue, the further weakening of state authority could accelerate Al-Shabaab’s expansion from rural areas into cities. The Role of International Partners International partners bear partial responsibility for this state of affairs. Turkey has become one of Mohamud’s most prominent bilateral security partners, providing military training, equipment, and support to Somali forces for more than a decade and with no accountability. The TURKSOM Military Training Academy has trained thousands of Somali soldiers, including members of the elite Gorgor Commando Brigade. The United States has continued to provide military assistance, with AFRICOM Commander General Michael Langley reaffirming the United States’ commitment to supporting Somalia’s fight against terrorism. However, as a result of Somali Government’s failure to meaningfully engage war against Alshabab, the US communicated a definitive policy decision establishing December 31, 2026, as the termination date for all support to the United Nations Support Office in Somalia. By continuing to arm and train a federal army that is then deployed against member states and political opponents, the international community is inadvertently enabling the very internal conflicts that undermine the counterterrorism mission. The African Union has called for peaceful dialogue, warning that rising tensions risk undermining stability. But words of restraint are insufficient when military assistance continues without conditionality. A State at War with Itself Cannot Fight a Common Enemy The evidence is unambiguous. The Somali federal government, under President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, has systematically used internationally trained and equipped military forces to: 1. Attack Jubaland, suffering a catastrophic defeat at Raskamboni in December 2024, with 240 federal soldiers surrendering to regional forces; 2. Forcibly remove the elected president of Southwest State in March 2026, using Turkish-trained Gorgor special forces and Turkish-supplied drones; 3. Confront and suppress political opponents in Mogadishu in June 2026, killing at least 13 people and displacing 12,500 households; and 4. Escalate tensions with Puntland, leading to the routing of federal forces and the capture of 101 militiamen on August 5, 2026, all while Al-Shabaab seizes strategic towns and advances its insurgency. AUSSOM cannot clear Al-Shabaab without the Somali government’s full engagement in the fight. But the Somali government is not engaged, it is fighting its own member states and political rivals. As Jubaland stated, weapons and military equipment were being moved into peaceful areas while Somali forces fighting Al-Shabaab faced shortages of arms and supplies. The international community must recognize that military solutions alone cannot succeed where political unity is absent. It is therefore imperative that the international community prioritize resolving Somalia’s internal political problems as a prerequisite for any effective counterterrorism strategy. AUSSOM troop-contributing countries have been urged to make a political settlement the foundation for Somalia’s security arrangements and future governance. Somalia’s opposition leaders have appealed to African Union troop-contributing countries to prioritize an inclusive political settlement before implementing any further security transition. Until Somalia’s federal government and its member states are reconciled, until internationally provided military assets are used exclusively against Al-Shabaab rather than against political opponents, and until Somalia’s political class forges a united front against their common enemy, the fight against Al-Shabaab will continue to yield no fruits. Somalia, which is not with itself, cannot fight against Al-Shabaab. Djama Mahamoud Ali Email: djama_m@yahoo.om The post AUSSOM Cannot Eradicate Al-Shabaab Without Somali Government’s Full Engagement in the Fight appeared first on WardheerNews .
